column5: ultimate fright and stark madness wrenched from scores of human throats - a yell which came strong and clear despite the depth from which it must have burst; after which darkness and silence ruled all things. Spirals of acrid smoke ascended to blot out the stars

column1: Toward dawn two frightened messengers with monstrous and unplaceable odours saturating their clothing knocked at the Fenner door and requested a keg of rum

column7: whereby the letters were saved after all

column1: Not one man who participated in that terrible raid could ever be induced to say a word concerning it
column2: and every fragment of the vague data which survives comes from those outside the final fighting party. There is something frightful in the care with which these actual raiders destroyed each scrap which bore the least allusion to the matter. Eight sailors had been killed
column3: but although their bodies were not produced their families were satisfied with the statement that a clash with customs officers had occurred. The same statement also covered the numerous cases of wounds
column4: all of which were extensively bandaged and treated only by Dr. Jabez Bowen
column5: who had accompanied the party. Hardest to explain was the nameless odour clinging to all the raiders
column6: a thing which was discussed for weeks. Of the citizen leaders

column9: sobered
column10: and shaken. It is fortunate that they were all strong men of action and simple

column1: \VIII.

In the meantime a quieter yet even more spiritually poignant phase of the horror had been blackly unwinding itself behind the closed door of a shelf-lined room in Arkham. The curious manuscript record or diary of Wilbur Whateley
column2: delivered to Miskatonic University for translation
column3: had caused much worry and bafflement among the experts in languages both ancient and modern; its very alphabet
column4: notwithstanding a general resemblance to the heavily shaded Arabic used in Mesopotamia
column5: being absolutely unknown to any available authority. The final conclusion of the linguists was that the text represented an artificial alphabet
column6: giving the effect of a cipher; though none of the usual methods of cryptographic solution seemed to furnish any clue
column7: even when applied on the basis of every tongue the writer might conceivably have used. The ancient books taken from Whateley’s quarters
column8: while absorbingly interesting and in several cases promising to open up new and terrible lines of research among philosophers and men of science
column9: were of no assistance whatever in this matter. One of them
column10: a heavy tome with an iron clasp
column11: was in another unknown alphabet—this one of a very different cast
column12: and resembling Sanscrit more than anything else. The old ledger was at length given wholly into the charge of Dr. Armitage
column13: both because of his peculiar interest in the Whateley matter
column14: and because of his wide linguistic learning and skill in the mystical formulae of antiquity and the Middle Ages.

column1: Armitage had an idea that the alphabet might be something esoterically used by certain forbidden cults which have come down from old times
column2: and which have inherited many forms and traditions from the wizards of the Saracenic world. That question
column3: however
column4: he did not deem vital; since it would be unnecessary to know the origin of the symbols if
column5: as he suspected
column6: they were used as a cipher in a modern language. It was his belief that
column7: considering the great amount of text involved
column8: the writer would scarcely have wished the trouble of using another speech than his own
column9: save perhaps in certain special formulae and incantations. Accordingly he attacked the manuscript with the preliminary assumption that the bulk of it was in English.

column1: Dr. Armitage knew

column5: Giambattista Porta’s De Furtivis Literarum Notis
column6: De Vigenère’s Traité des Chiffres
column7: Falconer’s Cryptomenysis Patefacta

column10: von Marten
column11: and Klüber’s Kryptographik. He interspersed his study of the books with attacks on the manuscript itself

column14: and the message built up with arbitrary key-words known only to the initiated. The older authorities seemed rather more helpful than the newer ones
column15: and Armitage concluded that the code of the manuscript was one of great antiquity
column16: no doubt handed down through a long line of mystical experimenters. Several times he seemed near daylight
column17: only to be set back by some unforeseen obstacle. Then
column18: as September approached
column19: the clouds began to clear. Certain letters
column20: as used in certain parts of the manuscript
column21: emerged definitely and unmistakably; and it became obvious that the text was indeed in English.

column1: On the evening of September 2nd the last major barrier gave way
column2: and Dr. Armitage read for the first time a continuous passage of Wilbur Whateley’s annals. It was in truth a diary

column7: he remembered
column8: by a child of three and a half who looked like a lad of twelve or thirteen.

column1: “Today learned the Aklo for the Sabaoth
column2: ” it ran
column3: “which did not like
column4: it being answerable from the hill and not from the air. That upstairs more ahead of me than I had thought it would be
column5: and is not like to have much earth brain. Shot Elam Hutchins’ collie Jack when he went to bite me
column6: and Elam says he would kill me if he dast. I guess he won’t. Grandfather kept me saying the Dho formula last night

column12: and it is near like them at May-Eve on the Hill. The other face may wear off some. I wonder how I shall look when the earth is cleared and there are no earth beings on it. He that came with the Aklo Sabaoth said I may be transfigured
column13: there being much of outside to work on.”

column1: Morning found Dr. Armitage in a cold sweat of terror and a frenzy of wakeful concentration. He had not left the manuscript all night
column2: but sat at his table under the electric light turning page after page with shaking hands as fast as he could decipher the cryptic text. He had nervously telephoned his wife he would not be home
column3: and when she brought him a breakfast from the house he could scarcely dispose of a mouthful. All that day he read on
column4: now and then halted maddeningly as a reapplication of the complex key became necessary. Lunch and dinner were brought him
column5: but he ate only the smallest fraction of either. Toward the middle of the next night he drowsed off in his chair
column6: but soon woke out of a tangle of nightmares almost as hideous as the truths and menaces to man’s existence that he had uncovered.

column1: On the morning of September 4th Professor Rice and Dr. Morgan insisted on seeing him for a while
column2: and departed trembling and ashen-grey. That evening he went to bed
column3: but slept only fitfully. Wednesday—the next day—he was back at the manuscript
column4: and began to take copious notes both from the current sections and from those he had already deciphered. In the small hours of that night he slept a little in an easy-chair in his office
column5: but was at the manuscript again before dawn. Some time before noon his physician
column6: Dr. Hartwell
column7: called to see him and insisted that he cease work. He refused; intimating that it was of the most vital importance for him to complete the reading of the diary
column8: and promising an explanation in due course of time.

column1: That evening
column2: just as twilight fell
column3: he finished his terrible perusal and sank back exhausted. His wife
column4: bringing his dinner
column5: found him in a half-comatose state; but he was conscious enough to warn her off with a sharp cry when he saw her eyes wander toward the notes he had taken. Weakly rising
column6: he gathered up the scribbled papers and sealed them all in a great envelope

column8: but was so clearly in need of medical aid that Dr. Hartwell was summoned at once. As the doctor put him to bed he could only mutter over and over again
column9: “But what
column10: in God’s name
column11: can we do?”

column1: Dr. Armitage slept
column2: but was partly delirious the next day. He made no explanations to Hartwell
column3: but in his calmer moments spoke of the imperative need of a long conference with Rice and Morgan. His wilder wanderings were very startling indeed
column4: including frantic appeals that something in a boarded-up farmhouse be destroyed
column5: and fantastic references to some plan for the extirpation of the entire human race and all animal and vegetable life from the earth by some terrible elder race of beings from another dimension. He would shout that the world was in danger
column6: since the Elder Things wished to strip it and drag it away from the solar system and cosmos of matter into some other plane or phase of entity from which it had once fallen

column1: “Stop them
column2: stop them!” he would shout. “Those Whateleys meant to let them in
column3: and the worst of all is left! Tell Rice and Morgan we must do something—it’s a blind business
column4: but I know how to make the powder. . . . It hasn’t been fed since the second of August
column5: when Wilbur came here to his death
column6: and at that rate. . . .”

column1: But Armitage had a sound physique despite his seventy-three years
column2: and slept off his disorder that night without developing any real fever. He woke late Friday
column3: clear of head
column4: though sober with a gnawing fear and tremendous sense of responsibility. Saturday afternoon he felt able to go over to the library and summon Rice and Morgan for a conference
column5: and the rest of that day and evening the three men tortured their brains in the wildest speculation and the most desperate debate. Strange and terrible books were drawn voluminously from the stack shelves and from secure places of storage; and diagrams and formulae were copied with feverish haste and in bewildering abundance. Of scepticism there was none. All three had seen the body of Wilbur Whateley as it lay on the floor in a room of that very building
column6: and after that not one of them could feel even slightly inclined to treat the diary as a madman’s raving.

column2: and the negative finally won. There were things involved which simply could not be believed by those who had not seen a sample
column3: as indeed was made clear during certain subsequent investigations. Late at night the conference disbanded without having developed a definite plan

column5: the more he was inclined to doubt the efficacy of any material agent in stamping out the entity which Wilbur Whateley had left behind him—the earth-threatening entity which
column6: unknown to him
column7: was to burst forth in a few hours and become the memorable Dunwich horror.

column4: and believed he would try a trip to Dunwich within a week. Then

column7: telling what a record-breaking monster the bootleg whiskey of Dunwich had raised up. Armitage

column1: Ward spent most of his time at the bungalow
column2: but slept occasionally at home and was still reckoned a dweller beneath his father's roof. Twice he was absent from the city on week-long trips

column4: and lacked some of his former assurance when repeating to Dr. Willett his old
column5: old story of vital research and future revelations. Willett often waylaid him at his father's house
column6: for the elder Ward was deeply worried and perplexed
column7: and wished his son to get as much sound oversight as could be managed in the case of so secretive and independent an adult. The doctor still insists that the youth was sane even as late as this

column1: About September the vampirism declined
column2: but in the following January Ward almost became involved in serious trouble. For some time the nocturnal arrival and departure of motor trucks at the Pawtuxet bungalow had been commented upon
column3: and at this juncture an unforeseen hitch exposed the nature of at least one item of their contents. In a lonely spot near Hope Valley had occurred one of the frequent sordid waylayings of trucks by ""hi-jackers"" in quest of liquor shipments
column4: but this time the robbers had been destined to receive the greater shock. For the long cases they seized proved upon opening to contain some exceedingly gruesome things; so gruesome
column5: in fact
column6: that the matter could not be kept quiet amongst the denizens of the underworld. The thieves had hastily buried what they discovered

column8: under promise of immunity from prosecution on any additional charge

It would not be well for the national - or even the international - sense of decorum if the public were ever to know what was uncovered by that awestruck party. There was no mistaking it
column10: even by these far from studious officers; and telegrams to Washington ensued with feverish rapidity.

column1: The cases were addressed to Charles Ward at his Pawtuxet bungalow
column2: and State and Federal officials at once paid him a very forceful and serious call. They found him pallid and worried with his two odd companions
column3: and received from him what seemed to be a valid explanation and evidence of innocence. He had needed certain anatomical specimens as part of a programme of research whose depth and genuineness anyone who had known him in the last decade could prove
column4: and had ordered the required kind and number from agencies which he had thought as reasonably legitimate as such things can be. Of the identity of the specimens he had known absolutely nothing
column5: and was properly shocked when the inspectors hinted at the monstrous effect on public sentiment and national dignity which a knowledge of the matter would produce. In this statement he was firmly sustained by his bearded colleague Dr. Allen
column6: whose oddly hollow voice carried even more conviction than his own nervous tones; so that in the end the officials took no action
column7: but carefully set down the New York name and address which Ward gave them as a basis for a search which came to nothing. It is only fair to add that the specimens were quickly and quietly restored to their proper places
column8: and that the general public will never know of their blasphemous disturbance.

column1: On February 9
column3: Dr. Willett received a letter from Charles Ward which he considers of extraordinary importance

column1: 100 Prospect St.
Providence
column2: R.I.

column1: February 8
Dear Dr. Willett: -
""I feel that at last the time has come for me to make the disclosures which I have so long promised you
column2: and for which you have pressed me so often. The patience you have shewn in waiting
column3: and the confidence you have shewn in my mind and integrity
column4: are things I shall never cease to appreciate.

column1: ""And now that I am ready to speak
column2: I must own with humiliation that no triumph such as I dreamed of can ever be mine. Instead of triumph I have found terror
column3: and my talk with you will not be a boast of victory but a plea for help and advice in saving both myself and the world from a horror beyond all human conception or calculation. You recall what those Fenner letters said of the old raiding party at Pawtuxet. That must all be done again
column4: and quickly. Upon us depends more than can be put into words - all civilisation
column5: all natural law
column6: perhaps even the fate of the solar system and the universe. I have brought to light a monstrous abnormality
column7: but I did it for the sake of knowledge. Now for the sake of all life and Nature you must help me thrust it back into the dark again.

column1: ""I have left that Pawtuxet place forever
column2: and we must extirpate everything existing there
column3: alive or dead. I shall not go there again
column4: and you must not believe it if you ever hear that I am there. I will tell you why I say this when I see you. I have come home for good
column5: and wish you would call on me at the very first moment that you can spare five or six hours continuously to hear what I have to say. It will take that long - and believe me when I tell you that you never had a more genuine professional duty than this. My life and reason are the very least things which hang in the balance.

column1: ""I dare not tell my father
column2: for he could not grasp the whole thing. But I have told him of my danger
column3: and he has four men from a detective agency watching the house. I don't know how much good they can do
column4: for they have against them forces which even you could scarcely envisage or acknowledge. So come quickly if you wish to see me alive and hear how you may help to save the cosmos from stark hell.

column1: ""Any time will do - I shall not be out of the house. Don't telephone ahead
column2: for there is no telling who or what may try to intercept you. And let us pray to whatever gods there be that nothing may prevent this meeting.

column1: ""In utmost gravity and desperation
Charles Dexter Ward.""
P.S. Shoot Dr. Allen on sight and dissolve his body in acid. Don't burn it.""

column6: ancient
column7: and horrible was hovering about he felt quite sure

column9: but had heard much of his aspect and bearing

column6: ""I can't receive anyone for some time

column5: and the sunset cheer gave place to a vague growing terror which flew shadow-like before the night. Mr. Ward finally arrived

column8: and urged his caller to do all he could to restore the boy to normal poise. Willett was glad to escape from that library

column1: The next morning Willett received a message from the senior Ward
column2: saying that Charles was still absent. Mr. Ward mentioned that Dr. Allen had telephoned him to say that Charles would remain at Pawtuxet for some time
column3: and that he must not be disturbed. This was necessary because Allen himself was suddenly called away for an indefinite period

column7: but which was disturbing to the point of fearfulness.

column1: Faced by these baffling and contradictory reports
column2: Dr. Willett was frankly at a loss what to do. The frantic earnestness of Charles's note was not to be denied
column3: yet what could one think of its writer's immediate violation of his own expressed policy? Young Ward had written that his delvings had become blasphemous and menacing
column4: that they and his bearded colleague must be extirpated at any cost
column5: and that he himself would never return to their final scene; yet according to latest advices he had forgotten all this and was back in the thick of the mystery. Common sense bade one leave the youth alone with his freakishness
column6: yet some deeper instinct would not permit the impression of that frenzied letter to subside. Willett read it over again

column8: and in conjunction with what the doctor already knew evoked too vivid hints of monstrosities from beyond time and space to permit of any cynical explanation. There were nameless horrors abroad; and no matter how little one might be able to get at them
column9: one ought to stand prepared for any sort of action at any time.

column1: For over a week Dr. Willett pondered on the dilemma which seemed thrust upon him
column2: and became more and more inclined to pay Charles a call at the Pawtuxet bungalow. No friend of the youth had ever ventured to storm this forbidden retreat
column3: and even his father knew of its interior only from such descriptions as he chose to give; but Willett felt that some direct conversation with his patient was necessary. Mr. Ward had been receiving brief and non-committal typed notes from his son
column4: and said that Mrs. Ward in her Atlantic City retirement had had no better word. So at length the doctor resolved to act; and despite a curious sensation inspired by old legends of Joseph Curwen
column5: and by more recent revelations and warnings from Charles Ward
column6: set boldly out for the bungalow on the bluff above the river.

column1: Willett had visited the spot before through sheer curiosity
column2: though of course never entering the house or proclaiming his presence; hence knew exactly the route to take. Driving out Broad Street one early afternoon toward the end of February in his small motor
column3: he thought oddly of the grim party which had taken that selfsame road a hundred and fifty-seven years before on a terrible errand which none might ever comprehend.

column1: The ride through the city's decaying fringe was short
column2: and trim Edgewood and sleepy Pawtuxet presently spread out ahead. Willett turned to the right down Lockwood Street and drove his car as far along that rural road as he could
column3: then alighted and walked north to where the bluff towered above the lovely bends of the river and the sweep of misty downlands beyond. Houses were still few here
column4: and there was no mistaking the isolated bungalow with its concrete garage on a high point of land at his left. Stepping briskly up the neglected gravel walk he rapped at the door with a firm hand

column1: He must
column2: he said
column3: see Charles Ward at once on vitally important business. No excuse would be accepted
column4: and a repulse would mean only a full report of the matter to the elder Ward. The mulatto still hesitated
column5: and pushed against the door when Willett attempted to open it; but the doctor merely raised his voice and renewed his demands. Then there came from the dark interior a husky whisper which somehow chilled the hearer through and through though he did not know why he feared it. ""Let him in
column6: Tony
column7: it said

column1: The minuteness with which Dr. Willett recalled and recorded his conversation of that afternoon is due to the importance he assigns to this particular period. For at last he concedes a vital change in Charles Dexter Ward's mentality
column2: and believes that the youth now spoke from a brain hopelessly alien to the brain whose growth he had watched for six and twenty years. Controversy with Dr. Lyman has compelled him to be very specific
column3: and he definitely dates the madness of Charles Ward from the time the typewritten notes began to reach his parents. Those notes are not in Ward's normal style; not even in the style of that last frantic letter to Willett. Instead
column4: they are strange and archaic
column5: as if the snapping of the writer's mind had released a flood of tendencies and impressions picked up unconsciously through boyhood antiquarianism. There is an obvious effort to be modern
column6: but the spirit and occasionally the language are those of the past.

column1: The past
column2: too
column3: was evident in Ward's every tone and gesture as he received the doctor in that shadowy bungalow. He bowed
column4: motioned Willett to a seat
column5: and began to speak abruptly in that strange whisper which he sought to explain at the very outset.

column1: ""I am grown phthisical
column2: he began
column3: ""from this cursed river air. You must excuse my speech. I suppose you are come from my father to see what ails me
column4: and I hope you will say nothing to alarm him.""

column1: Willett was studying these scraping tones with extreme care

column3: he felt
column4: was wrong; and he thought of what the family had told him about the fright of that Yorkshire butler one night. He wished it were not so dark

column1: ""I was coming to that
column2: the host replied. ""You must know
column3: I am in a very bad state of nerves
column4: and do and say queer things I cannot account for. As I have told you often
column5: I am on the edge of great matters; and the bigness of them has a way of making me light-headed. Any man might well be frighted of what I have found

column4: and the arts by reason of the doors I have access to. My ancestor had all this when those witless peeping Toms came and murdered him. I now have it again

column7: Sir
column8: and have no fear of this place or any in it. Dr. Allen is a man of fine parts

column1: Ward paused
column2: and the doctor hardly knew what to say or think. He felt almost foolish in the face of this calm repudiation of the letter; and yet there clung to him the fact that while the present discourse was strange and alien and indubitably mad

column4: and recall to the youth some past events which would restore a familiar mood; but in this process he obtained only the most grotesque results. It was the same with all the alienists later on. Important sections of Charles Ward's store of mental images
column5: mainly those touching modern times and his own personal life

column7: and he tried his best to hide it. When Willett would mention some favourite object of his boyhood archaistic studies he often shed by pure accident such a light as no normal mortal could conceivably be expected to possess

column1: It was not wholesome to know so much about the way the fat sheriff's wig fell off as he leaned over at the play in Mr. Douglass' Histrionick Academy in King Street on the eleventh of February
column3: which fell on a Thursday; or about how the actors cut the text of Steele's Conscious Lovers so badly that one was almost glad the Baptist-ridden legislature closed the theatre a fortnight later. That Thomas Sabin's Boston coach was ""damn'd uncomfortable"" old letters may well have told; but what healthy antiquarian could recall how the creaking of Epenetus Olney's new signboard (the gaudy crown he set up after he took to calling his tavern the Crown Coffee House) was exactly like the first few notes of the new jazz piece all the radios in Pawtuxet were playing?

column2: however
column3: would not be quizzed long in this vein. Modern and personal topics he waved aside quite summarily

That at least two living men - and one other of whom they dared not think - were in absolute possession of minds or personalities which had functioned as early as 1690 or before was likewise almost unassailably proved even in the face of all known natural laws. column1: But of the greatest immediate interest was the Orne material. It took Ward only a short time to prove from identity of penmanship a thing he had already considered established from the text of the letter to Curwen; namely

column7: and furnace-tending services. To find

column12: frankly baffled him; though he noted with a thrill of curiosity that the Biblical passage referred to - Job 14

column14: ""If a man die

column1: Young Ward came home in a state of pleasant excitement
column2: and spent the following Saturday in a long and exhaustive study of the house in Olney Court. The place
column3: now crumbling with age
column4: had never been a mansion; but was a modest two-and-a-half story wooden town house of the familiar Providence colonial type
column5: with plain peaked roof
column6: large central chimney
column7: and artistically carved doorway with rayed fanlight
column8: triangular pediment
column9: and trim Doric pilasters. It had suffered but little alteration externally

column1: The present negro inhabitants were known to him
column2: and he was very courteously shewn about the interior by old Asa and his stout wife Hannah. Here there was more change than the outside indicated
column3: and Ward saw with regret that fully half of the fine scroll-and-urn overmantels and shell-carved cupboard linings were gone
column4: whilst much of the fine wainscotting and bolection moulding was marked
column5: hacked
column6: and gouged
column7: or covered up altogether with cheap wall-paper. In general
column8: the survey did not yield as much as Ward had somehow expected; but it was at least exciting to stand within the ancestral walls which had housed such a man of horror as Joseph Curwen. He saw with a thrill that a monogram had been very carefully effaced from the ancient brass knocker.

column1: From then until after the close of school Ward spent his time on the photostatic copy of the Hutchinson cipher and the accumulation of local Curwen data. The former still proved unyielding; but of the latter he obtained so much
column2: and so many clues to similar data elsewhere
column3: that he was ready by July to make a trip to New London and New York to consult old letters whose presence in those places was indicated. This trip was very fruitful
column4: for it brought him the Fenner letters with their terrible description of the Pawtuxet farmhouse raid
column5: and the Nightingale-Talbot letters in which he learned of the portrait painted on a panel of the Curwen library. This matter of the portrait interested him particularly
column6: since he would have given much to know just what Joseph Curwen looked like; and he decided to make a second search of the house in Olney Court to see if there might not be some trace of the ancient features beneath peeling coats of later paint or layers of mouldy wall-paper.

column1: Early in August that search took place
column2: and Ward went carefully over the walls of every room sizeable enough to have been by any possibility the library of the evil builder. He paid especial attention to the large panels of such overmantels as still remained; and was keenly excited after about an hour
column3: when on a broad area above the fireplace in a spacious ground-floor room he became certain that the surface brought out by the peeling of several coats of paint was sensibly darker than any ordinary interior paint or the wood beneath it was likely to have been. A few more careful tests with a thin knife
column4: and he knew that he had come upon an oil portrait of great extent. With truly scholarly restraint the youth did not risk the damage which an immediate attempt to uncover the hidden picture with the knife might have done
column5: but just retired from the scene of his discovery to enlist expert help. In three days he returned with an artist of long experience
column6: Mr. Walter C. Dwight
column7: whose studio is near the foot of College Hill; and that accomplished restorer of paintings set to work at once with proper methods and chemical substances. Old Asa and his wife were duly excited over their strange visitors
column8: and were properly reimbursed for this invasion of their domestic hearth.

column1: As day by day the work of restoration progressed
column2: Charles Ward looked on with growing interest at the lines and shades gradually unveiled after their long oblivion. Dwight had begun at the bottom; hence since the picture was a three-quarter-length one
column3: the face did not come out for some time. It was meanwhile seen that the subject was a spare
column4: well-shaped man with dark-blue coat
column5: embroidered waistcoat
column6: black satin small-clothes
column7: and white silk stockings
column8: seated in a carved chair against the background of a window with wharves and ships beyond. When the head came out it was observed to bear a neat Albemarle wig
column9: and to possess a thin
column10: calm
column11: undistinguished face which seemed somehow familiar to both Ward and the artist. Only at the very last
column12: though
column13: did the restorer and his client begin to gasp with astonishment at the details of that lean
column14: pallid visage
column15: and to recognise with a touch of awe the dramatic trick which heredity had played. For it took the final bath of oil and the final stroke of the delicate scraper to bring out fully the expression which centuries had hidden; and to confront the bewildered Charles Dexter Ward
column16: dweller in the past
column17: with his own living features in the countenance of his horrible great-great-great-grandfather.

column1: Ward brought his parents to see the marvel he had uncovered
column2: and his father at once determined to purchase the picture despite its execution on stationary panelling. The resemblance to the boy
column3: despite an appearance of rather greater age
column4: was marvellous; and it could be seen that through some trick of atavism the physical contours of Joseph Curwen had found precise duplication after a century and a half. Mrs. Ward's resemblance to her ancestor was not at all marked
column5: though she could recall relatives who had some of the facial characteristics shared by her son and by the bygone Curwen. She did not relish the discovery
column6: and told her husband that he had better burn the picture instead of bringing it home. There was
column7: she averred
column8: something unwholesome about it; not only intrinsically
column9: but in its very resemblance to Charles. Mr. Ward
column10: however
column11: was a practical man of power and affairs - a cotton manufacturer with extensive mills at Riverpoint in the Pawtuxet Valley - and not one to listen to feminine scruples. The picture impressed him mightily with its likeness to his son
column12: and he believed the boy deserved it as a present. In this opinion
column13: it is needless to say
column14: Charles most heartily concurred; and a few days later Mr. Ward located the owner of the house - a small rodent-featured person with a guttural accent - and obtained the whole mantel and overmantel bearing the picture at a curtly fixed priced which cut short the impending torrent of unctuous haggling.

column1: It now remained to take off the panelling and remove it to the Ward home
column2: where provisions were made for its thorough restoration and installation with an electric mock-fireplace in Charles's third-floor study or library. To Charles was left the task of superintending this removal
column3: and on the twenty-eighth of August he accompanied two expert workmen from the Crooker decorating firm to the house in Olney Court
column4: where the mantel and portrait-bearing overmantel were detached with great care and precision for transportation in the company's motor truck. There was left a space of exposed brickwork marking the chimney's course
column5: and in this young Ward observed a cubical recess about a foot square
column6: which must have lain directly behind the head of the portrait. Curious as to what such a space might mean or contain
column7: the youth approached and looked within; finding beneath the deep coatings of dust and soot some loose yellowed papers
column8: a crude
column9: thick copybook
column10: and a few mouldering textile shreds which may have formed the ribbon binding the rest together. Blowing away the bulk of the dirt and cinders
column11: he took up the book and looked at the bold inscription on its cover. It was in a hand which he had learned to recognise at the Essex Institute
column12: and proclaimed the volume as the ""Journall and Notes of Jos: Curwen
column13: Gent.
column14: of Providence-Plantations
column15: Late of Salem.""

column1: Excited beyond measure by his discovery

column3: and Dr. Willett relies on them to help establish his theory that the youth was not mad when he began his major eccentricities. All the other papers were likewise in Curwen's handwriting
column4: and one of them seemed especially portentous because of its inscription: ""To Him Who Shal Come After
column5: & How He May Gett Beyonde Time & ye Spheres."" Another was in a cipher; the same
column6: Ward hoped
column7: as the Hutchinson cipher which had hitherto baffled him. A third

column10: Armiger"" and ""Jedediah Orne
column11: Esq.""
column12: 'or Their Heir or Heirs
column13: or Those Represent'g Them'. The sixth and last was inscribed: ""Joseph Curwen his Life and Travells Bet'n ye yeares 1678 and 1687: Of Whither He Voyag'd
column14: Where He Stay'd

column1: We have now reached the point from which the more academic school of alienists date Charles Ward's madness. Upon his discovery the youth had looked immediately at a few of the inner pages of the book and manuscripts
column2: and had evidently seen something which impressed him tremendously. Indeed
column3: in shewing the titles to the workmen he appeared to guard the text itself with peculiar care
column4: and to labour under a perturbation for which even the antiquarian and genealogical significance of the find could hardly account. Upon returning home he broke the news with an almost embarrassed air
column5: as if he wished to convey an idea of its supreme importance without having to exhibit the evidence itself. He did not even shew the titles to his parents
column6: but simply told them that he had found some documents in Joseph Curwen's handwriting
column7: ""mostly in cipher""
column8: which would have to be studied very carefully before yielding up their true meaning. It is unlikely that he would have shewn what he did to the workmen
column9: had it not been for their unconcealed curiosity. As it was he doubtless wished to avoid any display of peculiar reticence which would increase their discussion of the matter.

column1: That night Charles Ward sat up in his room reading the new-found book and papers
column2: and when day came he did not desist. His meals
column3: on his urgent request when his mother called to see what was amiss
column4: were sent up to him; and in the afternoon he appeared only briefly when the men came to install the Curwen picture and mantelpiece in his study. The next night he slept in snatches in his clothes
column5: meanwhile wrestling feverishly with the unravelling of the cipher manuscript. In the morning his mother saw that he was at work on the photostatic copy of the Hutchinson cipher
column6: which he had frequently shewn her before; but in response to her query he said that the Curwen key could not be applied to it. That afternoon he abandoned his work and watched the men fascinatedly as they finished their installation of the picture with its woodwork above a cleverly realistic electric log
column7: setting the mock-fireplace and overmantel a little out from the north wall as if a chimney existed
column8: and boxing in the sides with panelling to match the room's. The front panel holding the picture was sawn and hinged to allow cupboard space behind it. After the workmen went he moved his work into the study and sat down before it with his eyes half on the cipher and half on the portrait which stared back at him like a year-adding and century-recalling mirror.

column1: His parents
column2: subsequently recalling his conduct at this period
column3: give interesting details anent the policy of concealment which he practiced. Before servants he seldom hid any paper which he might be studying
column4: since he rightly assumed that Curwen's intricate and archaic chirography would be too much for them. With his parents
column5: however
column6: he was more circumspect; and unless the manuscript in question were a cipher
column7: or a mere mass of cryptic symbols and unknown ideographs (as that entitled ""To Him Who Shal Come After etc."" seemed to be)
column8: he would cover it with some convenient paper until his caller had departed. At night he kept the papers under lock and key in an antique cabinet of his
column9: where he also placed them whenever he left the room. He soon resumed fairly regular hours and habits
column10: except that his long walks and other outside interests seemed to cease. The opening of school
column11: where he now began his senior year
column12: seemed a great bore to him; and he frequently asserted his determination never to bother with college. He had
column13: he said
column14: important special investigations to make
column15: which would provide him with more avenues toward knowledge and the humanities than any university which the world could boast.

column1: Naturally
column2: only one who had always been more or less studious
column3: eccentric
column4: and solitary could have pursued this course for many days without attracting notice. Ward
column5: however
column6: was constitutionally a scholar and a hermit; hence his parents were less surprised than regretful at the close confinement and secrecy he adopted. At the same time
column7: both his father and mother thought it odd that he would shew them no scrap of his treasure-trove
column8: nor give any connected account of such data as he had deciphered. This reticence he explained away as due to a wish to wait until he might announce some connected revelation

column1: During October Ward began visiting the libraries again
column2: but no longer for the antiquarian matter of his former days. Witchcraft and magic
column3: occultism and daemonology
column4: were what he sought now; and when Providence sources proved unfruitful he would take the train for Boston and tap the wealth of the great library in Copley Square
column5: the Widener Library at Harvard
column6: or the Zion Research Library in Brookline
column7: where certain rare works on Biblical subjects are available. He bought extensively

column1: About the middle of January
column3: there entered Ward's bearing an element of triumph which he did not explain
column4: and he was no more found at work upon the Hutchinson cipher. Instead
column5: he inaugurated a dual policy of chemical research and record-scanning; fitting up for the one a laboratory in the unused attic of the house
column6: and for the latter haunting all the sources of vital statistics in Providence. Local dealers in drugs and scientific supplies
column7: later questioned
column8: gave astonishingly queer and meaningless catalogues of the substances and instruments he purchased; but clerks at the State House
column9: the City Hall
column10: and the various libraries agree as to the definite object of his second interest. He was searching intensely and feverishly for the grave of Joseph Curwen
column11: from whose slate slab an older generation had so wisely blotted the name.

column1: Little by little there grew upon the Ward family the conviction that something was wrong. Charles had had freaks and changes of minor interests before
column2: but this growing secrecy and absorption in strange pursuits was unlike even him. His school work was the merest pretence; and although he failed in no test
column3: it could be seen that the old application had all vanished. He had other concernments now; and when not in his new laboratory with a score of obsolete alchemical books
column4: could be found either poring over old burial records down town or glued to his volumes of occult lore in his study
column5: where the startlingly - one almost fancied increasingly - similar features of Joseph Curwen stared blandly at him from the great overmantel on the north wall.

column1: Late in March Ward added to his archive-searching a ghoulish series of rambles about the various ancient cemeteries of the city. The cause appeared later
column2: when it was learned from City Hall clerks that he had probably found an important clue. His quest had suddenly shifted from the grave of Joseph Curwen to that of one Naphthali Field; and this shift was explained when
column3: upon going over the files that he had been over
column4: the investigators actually found a fragmentary record of Curwen's burial which had escaped the general obliteration
column5: and which stated that the curious leaden coffin had been interred ""10 ft. S. and 5 ft. W. of Naphthali Field's grave in ye - "". The lack of a specified burying-ground in the surviving entry greatly complicated the search
column6: and Naphthali Field's grave seemed as elusive as that of Curwen; but here no systematic effacement had existed
column7: and one might reasonably be expected to stumble on the stone itself even if its record had perished. Hence the rambles - from which St. John's (the former King's) Churchyard and the ancient Congregational burying-ground in the midst of Swan Point Cemetery were excluded
column8: since other statistics had shewn that the only Naphthali Field (obiit 1729) whose grave could have been meant had been a Baptist.

column1: It was toward May when Dr. Willett
column2: at the request of the senior Ward
column3: and fortified with all the Curwen data which the family had gleaned from Charles in his non-secretive days
column4: talked with the young man. The interview was of little value or conclusiveness
column5: for Willett felt at every moment that Charles was thoroughly master of himself and in touch with matters of real importance; but it at least forced the secretive youth to offer some rational explanation of his recent demeanour. Of a pallid
column6: impassive type not easily shewing embarrassment
column7: Ward seemed quite ready to discuss his pursuits
column8: though not to reveal their object. He stated that the papers of his ancestor had contained some remarkable secrets of early scientific knowledge
column9: for the most part in cipher
column10: of an apparent scope comparable only to the discoveries of Friar Bacon and perhaps surpassing even those. They were
column11: however
column12: meaningless except when correlated with a body of learning now wholly obsolete; so that their immediate presentation to a world equipped only with modern science would rob them of all impressiveness and dramatic significance. To take their vivid place in the history of human thought they must first be correlated by one familiar with the background out of which they evolved
column13: and to this task of correlation Ward was now devoting himself. He was seeking to acquire as fast as possible those neglected arts of old which a true interpreter of the Curwen data must possess
column14: and hoped in time to make a full announcement and presentation of the utmost interest to mankind and to the world of thought. Not even Einstein
column15: he declared
column16: could more profoundly revolutionise the current conception of things.

column1: As to his graveyard search
column2: whose object he freely admitted
column3: but the details of whose progress he did not relate
column4: he said he had reason to think that Joseph Curwen's mutilated headstone bore certain mystic symbols - carved from directions in his will and ignorantly spared by those who had effaced the name - which were absolutely essential to the final solution of his cryptic system. Curwen
column5: he believed
column6: had wished to guard his secret with care; and had consequently distributed the data in an exceedingly curious fashion. When Dr. Willett asked to see the mystic documents

column8: the cipher (title in cipher also)
column9: and the formula-filled message ""To Him Who Shal Come After"" - and let him glance inside such as were in obscure characters.

column4: lingered tenaciously in his memory. They ran: ""Ye Verse from Liber-Damnatus be'g spoke V Roodmasses and IV Hallows-Eves
column5: I am Hopeful ye Thing is breed'g Outside ye Spheres. It will drawe One who is to Come

column1: About this time the crafty scholar hit upon a last desperate expedient to regain his footing in the community. Hitherto a complete hermit

It may be that he also had deeper reasons for wishing an alliance; reasons so far outside the known cosmic sphere that only papers found a century and a half after his death caused anyone to suspect them; but of this nothing certain can ever be learned. Naturally he was aware of the horror and indignation with which any ordinary courtship of his would be received

column1: In 1766 came the final change in Joseph Curwen. It was very sudden
column2: and gained wide notice amongst the curious townsfolk; for the air of suspense and expectancy dropped like an old cloak
column3: giving instant place to an ill-concealed exaltation of perfect triumph. Curwen seemed to have difficulty in restraining himself from public harangues on what he had found or learned or made; but apparently the need of secrecy was greater than the longing to share his rejoicing
column4: for no explanation was ever offered by him. It was after this transition
column5: which appears to have come early in July
column6: that the sinister scholar began to astonish people by his possession of information which only their long-dead ancestors would seem to be able to impart.

column1: But Curwen's feverish secret activities by no means ceased with this change. On the contrary
column2: they tended rather to increase; so that more and more of his shipping business was handled by the captains whom he now bound to him by ties of fear as potent as those of bankruptcy had been. He altogether abandoned the slave trade
column3: alleging that its profits were constantly decreasing. Every possible moment was spent at the Pawtuxet farm; though there were rumours now and then of his presence in places which
column4: though not actually near graveyards
column5: were yet so situated in relation to graveyards that thoughtful people wondered just how thorough the old merchant's change of habits really was. Ezra Weeden
column6: though his periods of espionage were necessarily brief and intermittent on account of his sea voyaging
column7: had a vindictive persistence which the bulk of the practical townsfolk and farmers lacked; and subjected Curwen's affairs to a scrutiny such as they had never had before.

column1: Many of the odd manoeuvres of the strange merchant's vessels had been taken for granted on account of the unrest of the times

column6: who were carried down and across the bay and landed at an obscure point on the shore just north of Pawtuxet; being afterward driven up the bluff and across country to the Curwen farm

column13: silent docks

column17: and transport it overland to the farm; locking it in the same cryptical stone building which had formerly received the negroes. The cargo consisted almost wholly of boxes and cases

column1: Weeden always watched the farm with unremitting assiduity; visiting it each night for long periods
column2: and seldom letting a week go by without a sight except when the ground bore a footprint-revealing snow. Even then he would often walk as close as possible in the travelled road or on the ice of the neighbouring river to see what tracks others might have left. Finding his own vigils interrupted by nautical duties
column3: he hired a tavern companion named Eleazar Smith to continue the survey during his absences; and between them the two could have set in motion some extraordinary rumours. That they did not do so was only because they knew the effect of publicity would be to warn their quarry and make further progress impossible. Instead

column6: and what other diarists and letter-writers have timidly repeated from the statements which they finally made - and according to which the farm was only the outer shell of some vast and revolting menace

That at least two living men - and one other of whom they dared not think - were in absolute possession of minds or personalities which had functioned as early as 1690 or before was likewise almost unassailably proved even in the face of all known natural laws. What these horrible creatures - and Charles Ward as well - were doing or trying to do seemed fairly clear from their letters and from every bit of light both old and new which had filtered in upon the case. column1: A hideous traffick was going on among these nightmare ghouls

They had found unholy ways to keep their brains alive
column3: either in the same body or different bodies; and had evidently achieved a way of tapping the consciousness of the dead whom they gathered together. There had

column1: What hellish consciousness or voice
column2: what morbid shade or presence

column5: and the gossip

column1: The morning of April 6th dawned clear

column6: newly come to the Congregational Church at Dunwich Village
column7: preached a memorable sermon on the close presence of Satan and his imps; in which he said:

column1: “It must be allow’d
column2: that these Blasphemies of an infernall Train of Daemons are Matters of too common Knowledge to be deny’d; the cursed Voices of Azazel and Buzrael
column3: of Beelzebub and Belial
column4: being heard now from under Ground by above a Score of credible Witnesses now living. I my self did not more than a Fortnight ago catch a very plain Discourse of evill Powers in the Hill behind my House; wherein there were a Rattling and Rolling
column5: Groaning
column6: Screeching
column7: and Hissing
column8: such as no Things of this Earth cou’d raise up

column10: and only the Divell unlock.”

column1: Mr. Hoadley disappeared soon after delivering this sermon; but the text

column1: Other traditions tell of foul odours near the hill-crowning circles of stone pillars
column2: and of rushing airy presences to be heard faintly at certain hours from stated points at the bottom of the great ravines; while still others try to explain the Devil’s Hop Yard—a bleak
column3: blasted hillside where no tree
column4: shrub
column5: or grass-blade will grow. Then too
column6: the natives are mortally afraid of the numerous whippoorwills which grow vocal on warm nights. It is vowed that the birds are psychopomps lying in wait for the souls of the dying
column7: and that they time their eerie cries in unison with the sufferer’s struggling breath. If they can catch the fleeing soul when it leaves the body
column8: they instantly flutter away chittering in daemoniac laughter; but if they fail
column9: they subside gradually into a disappointed silence.

column1: These tales
column2: of course
column3: are obsolete and ridiculous; because they come down from very old times. Dunwich is indeed ridiculously old—older by far than any of the communities within thirty miles of it. South of the village one may still spy the cellar walls and chimney of the ancient Bishop house
column4: which was built before 1700; whilst the ruins of the mill at the falls
column5: built in 1806
column6: form the most modern piece of architecture to be seen. Industry did not flourish here
column7: and the nineteenth-century factory movement proved short-lived. Oldest of all are the great rings of rough-hewn stone columns on the hill-tops

column11: disregarding the absurd improbability of such a theory
column12: persist in believing the remains Caucasian.

Charles Ward
column2: as we have seen
column3: first learned in 1918 of his descent from Joseph Curwen. That he at once took an intense interest in everything pertaining to the bygone mystery is not to be wondered at; for every vague rumour that he had heard of Curwen now became something vital to himself

column1: In his first delvings there was not the slightest attempt at secrecy; so that even Dr. Lyman hesitates to date the youth's madness from any period before the close of 1919. He talked freely with his family - though his mother was not particularly pleased to own an ancestor like Curwen - and with the officials of the various museums and libraries he visited. In applying to private families for records thought to be in their possession he made no concealment of his object
column2: and shared the somewhat amused scepticism with which the accounts of the old diarists and letter-writers were regarded. He often expressed a keen wonder as to what really had taken place a century and a half before at that Pawtuxet farmhouse whose site he vainly tried to find
column3: and what Joseph Curwen really had been.

column1: When he came across the Smith diary and archives and encountered the letter from Jedediah Orne he decided to visit Salem and look up Curwen's early activities and connexions there
column2: which he did during the Easter vacation of 1919. At the Essex Institute
column3: which was well known to him from former sojourns in the glamorous old town of crumbling Puritan gables and clustered gambrel roofs
column4: he was very kindly received
column5: and unearthed there a considerable amount of Curwen data. He found that his ancestor was born in Salem-Village
column6: now Danvers
column7: seven miles from town
column8: on the eighteenth of February (O.S.) 1662-3; and that he had run away to sea at the age of fifteen
column9: not appearing again for nine years
column10: when he returned with the speech
column11: dress
column12: and manners of a native Englishman and settled in Salem proper. At that time he had little to do with his family
column13: but spent most of his hours with the curious books he had brought from Europe
column14: and the strange chemicals which came for him on ships from England
column15: France
column16: and Holland. Certain trips of his into the country were the objects of much local inquisitiveness
column17: and were whisperingly associated with vague rumours of fires on the hills at night.

column1: Curwen's only close friends had been one Edward Hutchinson of Salem-Village and one Simon Orne of Salem. With these men he was often seen in conference about the Common
column2: and visits among them were by no means infrequent. Hutchinson had a house well out toward the woods
column3: and it was not altogether liked by sensitive people because of the sounds heard there at night. He was said to entertain strange visitors
column4: and the lights seen from his windows were not always of the same colour. The knowledge he displayed concerning long-dead persons and long-forgotten events was considered distinctly unwholesome
column5: and he disappeared about the time the witchcraft panic began
column6: never to be heard from again. At that time Joseph Curwen also departed
column7: but his settlement in Providence was soon learned of. Simon Orne lived in Salem until 1720
column8: when his failure to grow visibly old began to excite attention. He thereafter disappeared
column9: though thirty years later his precise counterpart and self-styled son turned up to claim his property. The claim was allowed on the strength of documents in Simon Orne's known hand
column10: and Jedediah Orne continued to dwell in Salem till 1771
column11: when certain letters from Providence citizens to the Rev. Thomas Barnard and others brought about his quiet removal to parts unknown.

column8: that 'fortie Witches and the Blacke Man were wont to meete in the Woodes behind Mr. Hutchinson's house'
column9: and one Amity How declared at a session of August 8th before Judge Gedney that 'Mr. G. B. (Rev. George Burroughs) on that Nighte putt ye Divell his Marke upon Bridget S.
column10: Jonathan A.
column11: Simon O.

column13: Joseph C.
column14: Susan P.

column19: and began to work casually on the cipher as soon as it was delivered to him. After the following August his labours on the cipher became intense and feverish

column21: though

column1: But of the greatest immediate interest was the Orne material. It took Ward only a short time to prove from identity of penmanship a thing he had already considered established from the text of the letter to Curwen; namely

column3: it was hardly safe to live too long in Salem

column5: and did not return to claim his lands except as a representative of a new generation. Orne had apparently been careful to destroy most of his correspondence
column6: but the citizens who took action in 1771 found and preserved a few letters and papers which excited their wonder. There were cryptic formulae and diagrams in his and other hands which Ward now either copied with care or had photographed

column1: This Curwen letter

column1: This letter

column5: and was now the abode of a negro family much esteemed for occasional washing
column6: housecleaning
column7: and furnace-tending services. To find

column10: was a highly impressive thing to Ward; and he resolved to explore the place immediately upon his return. The more mystical phases of the letter
column11: which he took to be some extravagant kind of symbolism
column12: frankly baffled him; though he noted with a thrill of curiosity that the Biblical passage referred to - Job 14
column13: 14 - was the familiar verse
column14: ""If a man die
column15: shall he live again? All the days of my appointed time will I wait
column16: till my change come.""

column1: Young Ward came home in a state of pleasant excitement
column2: and spent the following Saturday in a long and exhaustive study of the house in Olney Court. The place
column3: now crumbling with age
column4: had never been a mansion; but was a modest two-and-a-half story wooden town house of the familiar Providence colonial type
column5: with plain peaked roof
column6: large central chimney
column7: and artistically carved doorway with rayed fanlight
column8: triangular pediment
column9: and trim Doric pilasters. It had suffered but little alteration externally

column1: The present negro inhabitants were known to him
column2: and he was very courteously shewn about the interior by old Asa and his stout wife Hannah. Here there was more change than the outside indicated
column3: and Ward saw with regret that fully half of the fine scroll-and-urn overmantels and shell-carved cupboard linings were gone
column4: whilst much of the fine wainscotting and bolection moulding was marked
column5: hacked
column6: and gouged
column7: or covered up altogether with cheap wall-paper. In general
column8: the survey did not yield as much as Ward had somehow expected; but it was at least exciting to stand within the ancestral walls which had housed such a man of horror as Joseph Curwen. He saw with a thrill that a monogram had been very carefully effaced from the ancient brass knocker.

column1: From then until after the close of school Ward spent his time on the photostatic copy of the Hutchinson cipher and the accumulation of local Curwen data. The former still proved unyielding; but of the latter he obtained so much
column2: and so many clues to similar data elsewhere
column3: that he was ready by July to make a trip to New London and New York to consult old letters whose presence in those places was indicated. This trip was very fruitful
column4: for it brought him the Fenner letters with their terrible description of the Pawtuxet farmhouse raid
column5: and the Nightingale-Talbot letters in which he learned of the portrait painted on a panel of the Curwen library. This matter of the portrait interested him particularly
column6: since he would have given much to know just what Joseph Curwen looked like; and he decided to make a second search of the house in Olney Court to see if there might not be some trace of the ancient features beneath peeling coats of later paint or layers of mouldy wall-paper.

column1: Early in August that search took place
column2: and Ward went carefully over the walls of every room sizeable enough to have been by any possibility the library of the evil builder. He paid especial attention to the large panels of such overmantels as still remained; and was keenly excited after about an hour
column3: when on a broad area above the fireplace in a spacious ground-floor room he became certain that the surface brought out by the peeling of several coats of paint was sensibly darker than any ordinary interior paint or the wood beneath it was likely to have been. A few more careful tests with a thin knife
column4: and he knew that he had come upon an oil portrait of great extent. With truly scholarly restraint the youth did not risk the damage which an immediate attempt to uncover the hidden picture with the knife might have done
column5: but just retired from the scene of his discovery to enlist expert help. In three days he returned with an artist of long experience
column6: Mr. Walter C. Dwight
column7: whose studio is near the foot of College Hill; and that accomplished restorer of paintings set to work at once with proper methods and chemical substances. Old Asa and his wife were duly excited over their strange visitors
column8: and were properly reimbursed for this invasion of their domestic hearth.

column1: As day by day the work of restoration progressed
column2: Charles Ward looked on with growing interest at the lines and shades gradually unveiled after their long oblivion. Dwight had begun at the bottom; hence since the picture was a three-quarter-length one
column3: the face did not come out for some time. It was meanwhile seen that the subject was a spare
column4: well-shaped man with dark-blue coat
column5: embroidered waistcoat
column6: black satin small-clothes
column7: and white silk stockings
column8: seated in a carved chair against the background of a window with wharves and ships beyond. When the head came out it was observed to bear a neat Albemarle wig
column9: and to possess a thin
column10: calm
column11: undistinguished face which seemed somehow familiar to both Ward and the artist. Only at the very last
column12: though
column13: did the restorer and his client begin to gasp with astonishment at the details of that lean
column14: pallid visage
column15: and to recognise with a touch of awe the dramatic trick which heredity had played. For it took the final bath of oil and the final stroke of the delicate scraper to bring out fully the expression which centuries had hidden; and to confront the bewildered Charles Dexter Ward
column16: dweller in the past
column17: with his own living features in the countenance of his horrible great-great-great-grandfather.

column1: Ward brought his parents to see the marvel he had uncovered
column2: and his father at once determined to purchase the picture despite its execution on stationary panelling. The resemblance to the boy
column3: despite an appearance of rather greater age
column4: was marvellous; and it could be seen that through some trick of atavism the physical contours of Joseph Curwen had found precise duplication after a century and a half. Mrs. Ward's resemblance to her ancestor was not at all marked
column5: though she could recall relatives who had some of the facial characteristics shared by her son and by the bygone Curwen. She did not relish the discovery
column6: and told her husband that he had better burn the picture instead of bringing it home. There was
column7: she averred
column8: something unwholesome about it; not only intrinsically
column9: but in its very resemblance to Charles. Mr. Ward
column10: however
column11: was a practical man of power and affairs - a cotton manufacturer with extensive mills at Riverpoint in the Pawtuxet Valley - and not one to listen to feminine scruples. The picture impressed him mightily with its likeness to his son
column12: and he believed the boy deserved it as a present. In this opinion
column13: it is needless to say
column14: Charles most heartily concurred; and a few days later Mr. Ward located the owner of the house - a small rodent-featured person with a guttural accent - and obtained the whole mantel and overmantel bearing the picture at a curtly fixed priced which cut short the impending torrent of unctuous haggling.

column1: It now remained to take off the panelling and remove it to the Ward home
column2: where provisions were made for its thorough restoration and installation with an electric mock-fireplace in Charles's third-floor study or library. To Charles was left the task of superintending this removal

column4: where the mantel and portrait-bearing overmantel were detached with great care and precision for transportation in the company's motor truck. There was left a space of exposed brickwork marking the chimney's course

column6: which must have lain directly behind the head of the portrait. Curious as to what such a space might mean or contain
column7: the youth approached and looked within; finding beneath the deep coatings of dust and soot some loose yellowed papers
column8: a crude

column10: and a few mouldering textile shreds which may have formed the ribbon binding the rest together. Blowing away the bulk of the dirt and cinders

column12: and proclaimed the volume as the ""Journall and Notes of Jos: Curwen
column13: Gent.
column14: of Providence-Plantations
column15: Late of Salem.""

column1: We have now reached the point from which the more academic school of alienists date Charles Ward's madness. Upon his discovery the youth had looked immediately at a few of the inner pages of the book and manuscripts
column2: and had evidently seen something which impressed him tremendously. Indeed
column3: in shewing the titles to the workmen he appeared to guard the text itself with peculiar care
column4: and to labour under a perturbation for which even the antiquarian and genealogical significance of the find could hardly account. Upon returning home he broke the news with an almost embarrassed air
column5: as if he wished to convey an idea of its supreme importance without having to exhibit the evidence itself. He did not even shew the titles to his parents
column6: but simply told them that he had found some documents in Joseph Curwen's handwriting
column7: ""mostly in cipher""
column8: which would have to be studied very carefully before yielding up their true meaning. It is unlikely that he would have shewn what he did to the workmen
column9: had it not been for their unconcealed curiosity. As it was he doubtless wished to avoid any display of peculiar reticence which would increase their discussion of the matter.

column1: That night Charles Ward sat up in his room reading the new-found book and papers
column2: and when day came he did not desist. His meals
column3: on his urgent request when his mother called to see what was amiss
column4: were sent up to him; and in the afternoon he appeared only briefly when the men came to install the Curwen picture and mantelpiece in his study. The next night he slept in snatches in his clothes
column5: meanwhile wrestling feverishly with the unravelling of the cipher manuscript. In the morning his mother saw that he was at work on the photostatic copy of the Hutchinson cipher
column6: which he had frequently shewn her before; but in response to her query he said that the Curwen key could not be applied to it. That afternoon he abandoned his work and watched the men fascinatedly as they finished their installation of the picture with its woodwork above a cleverly realistic electric log

column8: and boxing in the sides with panelling to match the room's. The front panel holding the picture was sawn and hinged to allow cupboard space behind it. After the workmen went he moved his work into the study and sat down before it with his eyes half on the cipher and half on the portrait which stared back at him like a year-adding and century-recalling mirror.

column1: His parents
column2: subsequently recalling his conduct at this period
column3: give interesting details anent the policy of concealment which he practiced. Before servants he seldom hid any paper which he might be studying
column4: since he rightly assumed that Curwen's intricate and archaic chirography would be too much for them. With his parents
column5: however
column6: he was more circumspect; and unless the manuscript in question were a cipher
column7: or a mere mass of cryptic symbols and unknown ideographs (as that entitled ""To Him Who Shal Come After etc."" seemed to be)
column8: he would cover it with some convenient paper until his caller had departed. At night he kept the papers under lock and key in an antique cabinet of his
column9: where he also placed them whenever he left the room. He soon resumed fairly regular hours and habits
column10: except that his long walks and other outside interests seemed to cease. The opening of school
column11: where he now began his senior year
column12: seemed a great bore to him; and he frequently asserted his determination never to bother with college. He had
column13: he said
column14: important special investigations to make
column15: which would provide him with more avenues toward knowledge and the humanities than any university which the world could boast.

column1: Naturally
column2: only one who had always been more or less studious
column3: eccentric
column4: and solitary could have pursued this course for many days without attracting notice. Ward
column5: however
column6: was constitutionally a scholar and a hermit; hence his parents were less surprised than regretful at the close confinement and secrecy he adopted. At the same time
column7: both his father and mother thought it odd that he would shew them no scrap of his treasure-trove
column8: nor give any connected account of such data as he had deciphered. This reticence he explained away as due to a wish to wait until he might announce some connected revelation
column9: but as the weeks passed without further disclosures there began to grow up between the youth and his family a kind of constraint; intensified in his mother's case by her manifest disapproval of all Curwen delvings.

column1: During October Ward began visiting the libraries again
column2: but no longer for the antiquarian matter of his former days. Witchcraft and magic
column3: occultism and daemonology
column4: were what he sought now; and when Providence sources proved unfruitful he would take the train for Boston and tap the wealth of the great library in Copley Square
column5: the Widener Library at Harvard
column6: or the Zion Research Library in Brookline
column7: where certain rare works on Biblical subjects are available. He bought extensively
column8: and fitted up a whole additional set of shelves in his study for newly acquired works on uncanny subjects; while during the Christmas holidays he made a round of out-of-town trips including one to Salem to consult certain records at the Essex Institute.

column1: About the middle of January
column3: there entered Ward's bearing an element of triumph which he did not explain
column4: and he was no more found at work upon the Hutchinson cipher. Instead
column5: he inaugurated a dual policy of chemical research and record-scanning; fitting up for the one a laboratory in the unused attic of the house
column6: and for the latter haunting all the sources of vital statistics in Providence. Local dealers in drugs and scientific supplies
column7: later questioned
column8: gave astonishingly queer and meaningless catalogues of the substances and instruments he purchased; but clerks at the State House
column9: the City Hall
column10: and the various libraries agree as to the definite object of his second interest. He was searching intensely and feverishly for the grave of Joseph Curwen
column11: from whose slate slab an older generation had so wisely blotted the name.

column1: Little by little there grew upon the Ward family the conviction that something was wrong. Charles had had freaks and changes of minor interests before
column2: but this growing secrecy and absorption in strange pursuits was unlike even him. His school work was the merest pretence; and although he failed in no test

column1: From then until after the close of school Ward spent his time on the photostatic copy of the Hutchinson cipher and the accumulation of local Curwen data. The former still proved unyielding; but of the latter he obtained so much

column1: Early in August that search took place

A few more careful tests with a thin knife

column1: We have now reached the point from which the more academic school of alienists date Charles Ward's madness. Upon his discovery the youth had looked immediately at a few of the inner pages of the book and manuscripts

column1: Late in March Ward added to his archive-searching a ghoulish series of rambles about the various ancient cemeteries of the city. The cause appeared later
column2: when it was learned from City Hall clerks that he had probably found an important clue. His quest had suddenly shifted from the grave of Joseph Curwen to that of one Naphthali Field; and this shift was explained when

column4: the investigators actually found a fragmentary record of Curwen's burial which had escaped the general obliteration

column7: and one might reasonably be expected to stumble on the stone itself even if its record had perished. Hence the rambles - from which St. John's (the former King's) Churchyard and the ancient Congregational burying-ground in the midst of Swan Point Cemetery were excluded

column6: impassive type not easily shewing embarrassment

column11: however
