column1: Not long after his mother's departure Charles Ward began negotiating for the Pawtuxet bungalow. It was a squalid little wooden edifice with a concrete garage
column2: perched high on the sparsely settled bank of the river slightly above Rhodes
column3: but for some odd reason the youth would have nothing else. He gave the real-estate agencies no peace till one of them secured it for him at an exorbitant price from a somewhat reluctant owner
column4: and as soon as it was vacant he took possession under cover of darkness
column5: transporting in a great closed van the entire contents of his attic laboratory
column6: including the books both weird and modern which he had borrowed from his study. He had this van loaded in the black small hours
column7: and his father recalls only a drowsy realisation of stifled oaths and stamping feet on the night the goods were taken away. After that Charles moved back to his own old quarters on the third floor
column8: and never haunted the attic again.

column1: To the Pawtuxet bungalow Charles transferred all the secrecy with which he had surrounded his attic realm
column2: save that he now appeared to have two sharers of his mysteries; a villainous-looking Portuguese half-caste from the South Main St. waterfront who acted as a servant
column3: and a thin
column4: scholarly stranger with dark glasses and a stubbly full beard of dyed aspect whose status was evidently that of a colleague. Neighbours vainly tried to engage these odd persons in conversation. The mulatto Gomes spoke very little English
column5: and the bearded man
column6: who gave his name as Dr. Allen
column7: voluntarily followed his example. Ward himself tried to be more affable
column8: but succeeded only in provoking curiosity with his rambling accounts of chemical research. Before long queer tales began to circulate regarding the all-night burning of lights; and somewhat later
column9: after this burning had suddenly ceased
column10: there rose still queerer tales of disproportionate orders of meat from the butcher's and of the muffled shouting
column11: declamation
column12: rhythmic chanting
column13: and screaming supposed to come from some very deep cellar below the place. Most distinctly the new and strange household was bitterly disliked by the honest bourgeoisie of the vicinity
column14: and it is not remarkable that dark hints were advanced connecting the hated establishment with the current epidemic of vampiristic attacks and murders; especially since the radius of that plague seemed now confined wholly to Pawtuxet and the adjacent streets of Edgewood.

column1: Ward spent most of his time at the bungalow
column2: but slept occasionally at home and was still reckoned a dweller beneath his father's roof. Twice he was absent from the city on week-long trips
column3: whose destinations have not yet been discovered. He grew steadily paler and more emaciated even than before
column4: and lacked some of his former assurance when repeating to Dr. Willett his old
column5: old story of vital research and future revelations. Willett often waylaid him at his father's house
column6: for the elder Ward was deeply worried and perplexed
column7: and wished his son to get as much sound oversight as could be managed in the case of so secretive and independent an adult. The doctor still insists that the youth was sane even as late as this
column8: and adduces many a conversation to prove his point.

column1: About September the vampirism declined
column2: but in the following January Ward almost became involved in serious trouble. For some time the nocturnal arrival and departure of motor trucks at the Pawtuxet bungalow had been commented upon
column3: and at this juncture an unforeseen hitch exposed the nature of at least one item of their contents. In a lonely spot near Hope Valley had occurred one of the frequent sordid waylayings of trucks by ""hi-jackers"" in quest of liquor shipments
column4: but this time the robbers had been destined to receive the greater shock. For the long cases they seized proved upon opening to contain some exceedingly gruesome things; so gruesome
column5: in fact
column6: that the matter could not be kept quiet amongst the denizens of the underworld. The thieves had hastily buried what they discovered
column7: but when the State Police got wind of the matter a careful search was made. A recently arrested vagrant
column8: under promise of immunity from prosecution on any additional charge
column9: at last consented to guide a party of troopers to the spot; and there was found in that hasty cache a very hideous and shameful thing. It would not be well for the national - or even the international - sense of decorum if the public were ever to know what was uncovered by that awestruck party. There was no mistaking it
column10: even by these far from studious officers; and telegrams to Washington ensued with feverish rapidity.

column1: The cases were addressed to Charles Ward at his Pawtuxet bungalow
column2: and State and Federal officials at once paid him a very forceful and serious call. They found him pallid and worried with his two odd companions
column3: and received from him what seemed to be a valid explanation and evidence of innocence. He had needed certain anatomical specimens as part of a programme of research whose depth and genuineness anyone who had known him in the last decade could prove
column4: and had ordered the required kind and number from agencies which he had thought as reasonably legitimate as such things can be. Of the identity of the specimens he had known absolutely nothing
column5: and was properly shocked when the inspectors hinted at the monstrous effect on public sentiment and national dignity which a knowledge of the matter would produce. In this statement he was firmly sustained by his bearded colleague Dr. Allen
column6: whose oddly hollow voice carried even more conviction than his own nervous tones; so that in the end the officials took no action
column7: but carefully set down the New York name and address which Ward gave them as a basis for a search which came to nothing. It is only fair to add that the specimens were quickly and quietly restored to their proper places
column8: and that the general public will never know of their blasphemous disturbance.

column1: On February 9
column3: Dr. Willett received a letter from Charles Ward which he considers of extraordinary importance
column4: and about which he has frequently quarrelled with Dr. Lyman. Lyman believes that this note contains positive proof of a well-developed case of dementia praecox
column5: but Willett on the other hand regards it as the last perfectly sane utterance of the hapless youth. He calls especial attention to the normal character of the penmanship; which though shewing traces of shattered nerves
column6: is nevertheless distinctly Ward's own. The text in full is as follows:

column1: 100 Prospect St.
Providence
column2: R.I.

column1: February 8
Dear Dr. Willett: -
""I feel that at last the time has come for me to make the disclosures which I have so long promised you
column2: and for which you have pressed me so often. The patience you have shewn in waiting
column3: and the confidence you have shewn in my mind and integrity
column4: are things I shall never cease to appreciate.

column1: ""And now that I am ready to speak
column2: I must own with humiliation that no triumph such as I dreamed of can ever be mine. Instead of triumph I have found terror
column3: and my talk with you will not be a boast of victory but a plea for help and advice in saving both myself and the world from a horror beyond all human conception or calculation. You recall what those Fenner letters said of the old raiding party at Pawtuxet. That must all be done again
column4: and quickly. Upon us depends more than can be put into words - all civilisation
column5: all natural law
column6: perhaps even the fate of the solar system and the universe. I have brought to light a monstrous abnormality
column7: but I did it for the sake of knowledge. Now for the sake of all life and Nature you must help me thrust it back into the dark again.

column1: ""I have left that Pawtuxet place forever
column2: and we must extirpate everything existing there
column3: alive or dead. I shall not go there again
column4: and you must not believe it if you ever hear that I am there. I will tell you why I say this when I see you. I have come home for good
column5: and wish you would call on me at the very first moment that you can spare five or six hours continuously to hear what I have to say. It will take that long - and believe me when I tell you that you never had a more genuine professional duty than this. My life and reason are the very least things which hang in the balance.

column1: ""I dare not tell my father
column2: for he could not grasp the whole thing. But I have told him of my danger
column3: and he has four men from a detective agency watching the house. I don't know how much good they can do
column4: for they have against them forces which even you could scarcely envisage or acknowledge. So come quickly if you wish to see me alive and hear how you may help to save the cosmos from stark hell.

column1: ""Any time will do - I shall not be out of the house. Don't telephone ahead
column2: for there is no telling who or what may try to intercept you. And let us pray to whatever gods there be that nothing may prevent this meeting.

column1: ""In utmost gravity and desperation
Charles Dexter Ward.""
P.S. Shoot Dr. Allen on sight and dissolve his body in acid. Don't burn it.""
Dr. Willett received this note about 10:30 a.m.
column2: and immediately arranged to spare the whole late afternoon and evening for the momentous talk
column3: letting it extend on into the night as long as might be necessary. He planned to arrive about four o'clock
column4: and through all the intervening hours was so engulfed in every sort of wild speculation that most of his tasks were very mechanically performed. Maniacal as the letter would have sounded to a stranger
column5: Willett had seen too much of Charles Ward's oddities to dismiss it as sheer raving. That something very subtle
column6: ancient
column7: and horrible was hovering about he felt quite sure
column8: and the reference to Dr. Allen could almost be comprehended in view of what Pawtuxet gossip said of Ward's enigmatical colleague. Willett had never seen the man
column9: but had heard much of his aspect and bearing
column10: and could not but wonder what sort of eyes those much-discussed dark glasses might conceal.

column4: one of the detectives said

column6: ""I can't receive anyone for some time
column7: you'll have to excuse me""
column8: ""Please postpone decisive action till we can arrange some sort of compromise""
column9: or ""I am very sorry
column10: but I must take a complete vacation from everything; I'll talk with you later"". Then
column11: apparently gaining boldness through meditation
column12: he had slipped out so quietly that no one had seen him depart or knew that he had gone until he returned about one o'clock and entered the house without a word. He had gone upstairs

column14: afterward trailing off into a kind of choking gasp. When
column15: however
column16: the butler had gone to inquire what the trouble was
column17: he had appeared at the door with a great show of boldness
column18: and had silently gestured the man away in a manner that terrified him unaccountably. Then he had evidently done some rearranging of his shelves

column20: but was told that there was none. The butler seemed queerly disturbed about something in Charles's appearance and manner
column21: and asked solicitously if there was much hope for a cure of his disordered nerves.

column1: For almost two hours Dr. Willett waited vainly in Charles Ward's library
column2: watching the dusty shelves with their wide gaps where books had been removed
column3: and smiling grimly at the panelled overmantel on the north wall
column4: whence a year before the suave features of old Joseph Curwen had looked mildly down. After a time the shadows began to gather
column5: and the sunset cheer gave place to a vague growing terror which flew shadow-like before the night. Mr. Ward finally arrived
column6: and shewed much surprise and anger at his son's absence after all the pains which had been taken to guard him. He had not known of Charles's appointment
column7: and promised to notify Willett when the youth returned. In bidding the doctor goodnight he expressed his utter perplexity at his son's condition
column8: and urged his caller to do all he could to restore the boy to normal poise. Willett was glad to escape from that library
column9: for something frightful and unholy seemed to haunt it; as if the vanished picture had left behind a legacy of evil. He had never liked that picture; and even now
column10: strong-nerved though he was
column11: there lurked a quality in its vacant panel which made him feel an urgent need to get out into the pure air as soon as possible.

column1: The next morning Willett received a message from the senior Ward
column2: saying that Charles was still absent. Mr. Ward mentioned that Dr. Allen had telephoned him to say that Charles would remain at Pawtuxet for some time
column3: and that he must not be disturbed. This was necessary because Allen himself was suddenly called away for an indefinite period
column4: leaving the researches in need of Charles's constant oversight. Charles sent his best wishes
column5: and regretted any bother his abrupt change of plans might have caused. In listening to this message Mr. Ward heard Dr. Allen's voice for the first time
column6: and it seemed to excite some vague and elusive memory which could not be actually placed
column7: but which was disturbing to the point of fearfulness.

column1: Faced by these baffling and contradictory reports
column2: Dr. Willett was frankly at a loss what to do. The frantic earnestness of Charles's note was not to be denied
column3: yet what could one think of its writer's immediate violation of his own expressed policy? Young Ward had written that his delvings had become blasphemous and menacing
column4: that they and his bearded colleague must be extirpated at any cost
column5: and that he himself would never return to their final scene; yet according to latest advices he had forgotten all this and was back in the thick of the mystery. Common sense bade one leave the youth alone with his freakishness
column6: yet some deeper instinct would not permit the impression of that frenzied letter to subside. Willett read it over again
column7: and could not make its essence sound as empty and insane as both its bombastic verbiage and its lack of fulfilment would seem to imply. Its terror was too profound and real
column8: and in conjunction with what the doctor already knew evoked too vivid hints of monstrosities from beyond time and space to permit of any cynical explanation. There were nameless horrors abroad; and no matter how little one might be able to get at them
column9: one ought to stand prepared for any sort of action at any time.

column1: For over a week Dr. Willett pondered on the dilemma which seemed thrust upon him
column2: and became more and more inclined to pay Charles a call at the Pawtuxet bungalow. No friend of the youth had ever ventured to storm this forbidden retreat
column3: and even his father knew of its interior only from such descriptions as he chose to give; but Willett felt that some direct conversation with his patient was necessary. Mr. Ward had been receiving brief and non-committal typed notes from his son
column4: and said that Mrs. Ward in her Atlantic City retirement had had no better word. So at length the doctor resolved to act; and despite a curious sensation inspired by old legends of Joseph Curwen
column5: and by more recent revelations and warnings from Charles Ward
column6: set boldly out for the bungalow on the bluff above the river.

column1: Willett had visited the spot before through sheer curiosity
column2: though of course never entering the house or proclaiming his presence; hence knew exactly the route to take. Driving out Broad Street one early afternoon toward the end of February in his small motor
column3: he thought oddly of the grim party which had taken that selfsame road a hundred and fifty-seven years before on a terrible errand which none might ever comprehend.

column1: The ride through the city's decaying fringe was short
column2: and trim Edgewood and sleepy Pawtuxet presently spread out ahead. Willett turned to the right down Lockwood Street and drove his car as far along that rural road as he could
column3: then alighted and walked north to where the bluff towered above the lovely bends of the river and the sweep of misty downlands beyond. Houses were still few here
column4: and there was no mistaking the isolated bungalow with its concrete garage on a high point of land at his left. Stepping briskly up the neglected gravel walk he rapped at the door with a firm hand
column5: and spoke without a tremor to the evil Portuguese mulatto who opened it to the width of a crack.

column1: He must
column2: he said
column3: see Charles Ward at once on vitally important business. No excuse would be accepted
column4: and a repulse would mean only a full report of the matter to the elder Ward. The mulatto still hesitated
column5: and pushed against the door when Willett attempted to open it; but the doctor merely raised his voice and renewed his demands. Then there came from the dark interior a husky whisper which somehow chilled the hearer through and through though he did not know why he feared it. ""Let him in
column6: Tony
column7: it said
column8: ""we may as well talk now as ever."" But disturbing as was the whisper
column9: the greater fear was that which immediately followed. The floor creaked and the speaker hove in sight - and the owner of those strange and resonant tones was seen to be no other than Charles Dexter Ward.

column1: The minuteness with which Dr. Willett recalled and recorded his conversation of that afternoon is due to the importance he assigns to this particular period. For at last he concedes a vital change in Charles Dexter Ward's mentality
column2: and believes that the youth now spoke from a brain hopelessly alien to the brain whose growth he had watched for six and twenty years. Controversy with Dr. Lyman has compelled him to be very specific
column3: and he definitely dates the madness of Charles Ward from the time the typewritten notes began to reach his parents. Those notes are not in Ward's normal style; not even in the style of that last frantic letter to Willett. Instead
column4: they are strange and archaic
column5: as if the snapping of the writer's mind had released a flood of tendencies and impressions picked up unconsciously through boyhood antiquarianism. There is an obvious effort to be modern
column6: but the spirit and occasionally the language are those of the past.

column1: The past
column2: too
column3: was evident in Ward's every tone and gesture as he received the doctor in that shadowy bungalow. He bowed
column4: motioned Willett to a seat
column5: and began to speak abruptly in that strange whisper which he sought to explain at the very outset.

column1: ""I am grown phthisical
column2: he began
column3: ""from this cursed river air. You must excuse my speech. I suppose you are come from my father to see what ails me
column4: and I hope you will say nothing to alarm him.""

column1: Willett was studying these scraping tones with extreme care
column2: but studying even more closely the face of the speaker. Something
column3: he felt
column4: was wrong; and he thought of what the family had told him about the fright of that Yorkshire butler one night. He wished it were not so dark
column5: but did not request that any blind be opened. Instead
column6: he merely asked Ward why he had so belied the frantic note of little more than a week before.

column1: ""I was coming to that
column2: the host replied. ""You must know
column3: I am in a very bad state of nerves
column4: and do and say queer things I cannot account for. As I have told you often
column5: I am on the edge of great matters; and the bigness of them has a way of making me light-headed. Any man might well be frighted of what I have found
column6: but I am not to be put off for long. I was a dunce to have that guard and stick at home; for having gone this far
column7: my place is here. I am not well spoke of by my prying neighbours
column8: and perhaps I was led by weakness to believe myself what they say of me. There is no evil to any in what I do
column9: so long as I do it rightly. Have the goodness to wait six months
column10: and I'll shew you what will pay your patience well.

column1: ""You may as well know I have a way of learning old matters from things surer than books
column2: and I'll leave you to judge the importance of what I can give to history
column3: philosophy
column4: and the arts by reason of the doors I have access to. My ancestor had all this when those witless peeping Toms came and murdered him. I now have it again
column5: or am coming very imperfectly to have a part of it. This time nothing must happen
column6: and least of all through any idiot fears of my own. Pray forget all I writ you
column7: Sir
column8: and have no fear of this place or any in it. Dr. Allen is a man of fine parts
column9: and I owe him an apology for anything ill I have said of him. I wish I had no need to spare him

column11: and I suppose that when I feared the work I feared him too as my greatest helper in it.""

column1: Ward paused
column2: and the doctor hardly knew what to say or think. He felt almost foolish in the face of this calm repudiation of the letter; and yet there clung to him the fact that while the present discourse was strange and alien and indubitably mad
column3: the note itself had been tragic in its naturalness and likeness to the Charles Ward he knew. Willett now tried to turn the talk on early matters
column4: and recall to the youth some past events which would restore a familiar mood; but in this process he obtained only the most grotesque results. It was the same with all the alienists later on. Important sections of Charles Ward's store of mental images
column5: mainly those touching modern times and his own personal life
column6: had been unaccountably expunged; whilst all the massed antiquarianism of his youth had welled up from some profound subconsciousness to engulf the contemporary and the individual. The youth's intimate knowledge of elder things was abnormal and unholy
column7: and he tried his best to hide it. When Willett would mention some favourite object of his boyhood archaistic studies he often shed by pure accident such a light as no normal mortal could conceivably be expected to possess
column8: and the doctor shuddered as the glib allusion glided by.

column1: It was not wholesome to know so much about the way the fat sheriff's wig fell off as he leaned over at the play in Mr. Douglass' Histrionick Academy in King Street on the eleventh of February
column3: which fell on a Thursday; or about how the actors cut the text of Steele's Conscious Lovers so badly that one was almost glad the Baptist-ridden legislature closed the theatre a fortnight later. That Thomas Sabin's Boston coach was ""damn'd uncomfortable"" old letters may well have told; but what healthy antiquarian could recall how the creaking of Epenetus Olney's new signboard (the gaudy crown he set up after he took to calling his tavern the Crown Coffee House) was exactly like the first few notes of the new jazz piece all the radios in Pawtuxet were playing?

column1: Ward
column2: however
column3: would not be quizzed long in this vein. Modern and personal topics he waved aside quite summarily
column4: whilst regarding antique affairs he soon shewed the plainest boredom. What he wished clearly enough was only to satisfy his visitor enough to make him depart without the intention of returning. To this end he offered to shew Willett the entire house
column5: and at once proceeded to lead the doctor through every room from cellar to attic. Willett looked sharply
column6: but noted that the visible books were far too few and trivial ever to have filled the wide gaps on Ward's shelves at home

column1: Mr. Ward now determined to call in person upon his son
column2: making it wholly a surprise visit. Dr. Willett took him in his car one evening

column1: Now definitely leagued together to do all they could toward the youth's mental salvation

column7: these quantities were quite absurd.

column3: and at times when the bungalow was dark. They might

column1: Such were the shreds and fragments gathered here and there; and over these Mr. Ward and Dr. Willett held many long and serious conferences. They strove to exercise deduction

column2: after all

column5: there could be no normal reason for this ill-concealed blankness on vital points. Moreover

After scanning this material and examining the ominous note to Willett they all agreed that Charles Ward's studies had been enough to unseat or at least to warp any ordinary intellect

column2: and has added a decade to the visible age of one whose youth was even then far behind. Dr. Willett had conferred at length with Mr. Ward
column3: and had come to an agreement with him on several points which both felt the alienists would ridicule. There was
column4: they conceded
column5: a terrible movement alive in the world
column6: whose direct connexion with a necromancy even older than the Salem witchcraft could not be doubted. That at least two living men - and one other of whom they dared not think - were in absolute possession of minds or personalities which had functioned as early as 1690 or before was likewise almost unassailably proved even in the face of all known natural laws. What these horrible creatures - and Charles Ward as well - were doing or trying to do seemed fairly clear from their letters and from every bit of light both old and new which had filtered in upon the case. They were robbing the tombs of all the ages
column7: including those of the world's wisest and greatest men
column8: in the hope of recovering from the bygone ashes some vestige of the consciousness and lore which had once animated and informed them.

column1: A hideous traffick was going on among these nightmare ghouls
column2: whereby illustrious bones were bartered with the calm calculativeness of schoolboys swapping books; and from what was extorted from this centuried dust there was anticipated a power and a wisdom beyond anything which the cosmos had ever seen concentrated in one man or group. They had found unholy ways to keep their brains alive
column3: either in the same body or different bodies; and had evidently achieved a way of tapping the consciousness of the dead whom they gathered together. There had
column4: it seems
column5: been some truth in chimerical old Borellus when he wrote of preparing from even the most antique remains certain ""Essential Saltes"" from which the shade of a long-dead living thing might be raised up. There was a formula for evoking such a shade
column6: and another for putting it down; and it had now been so perfected that it could be taught successfully. One must be careful about evocations
column7: for the markers of old graves are not always accurate.

column1: Willett and Mr. Ward shivered as they passed from conclusion to conclusion. Things - presences or voices of some sort - could be drawn down from unknown places as well as from the grave
column2: and in this process also one must be careful. Joseph Curwen had indubitably evoked many forbidden things
column3: and as for Charles - what might one think of him? What forces ""outside the spheres"" had reached him from Joseph Curwen's day and turned his mind on forgotten things? He had been led to find certain directions
column4: and he had used them. He had talked with the man of horror in Prague and stayed long with the creature in the mountains of Transylvania. And he must have found the grave of Joseph Curwen at last. That newspaper item and what his mother had heard in the night were too significant to overlook. Then he had summoned something
column5: and it must have come. That mighty voice aloft on Good Friday
column6: and those different tones in the locked attic laboratory. What were they like
column7: with their depth and hollowness? Was there not here some awful foreshadowing of the dreaded stranger Dr. Allen with his spectral bass? Yes
column8: that was what Mr. Ward had felt with vague horror in his single talk with the man - if man it were - over the telephone!

column1: What hellish consciousness or voice
column2: what morbid shade or presence
column3: had come to answer Charles Ward's secret rites behind that locked door? Those voices heard in argument - ""must have it red for three months"" - Good God! Was not that just before the vampirism broke out? The rifling of Ezra Weeden's ancient grave
column4: and the cries later at Pawtuxet - whose mind had planned the vengeance and rediscovered the shunned seat of elder blasphemies? And then the bungalow and the bearded stranger
column5: and the gossip
column6: and the fear. The final madness of Charles neither father nor doctor could attempt to explain
column7: but they did feel sure that the mind of Joseph Curwen had come to earth again and was following its ancient morbidities. Was daemoniac possession in truth a possibility? Allen had something to do with it
column8: and the detectives must find out more about one whose existence menaced the young man's life. In the meantime
column9: since the existence of some vast crypt beneath the bungalow seemed virtually beyond dispute
column10: some effort must be made to find it. Willett and Mr. Ward
column11: conscious of the sceptical attitude of the alienists
column12: resolved during their final conference to undertake a joint secret exploration of unparalleled thoroughness; and agreed to meet at the bungalow on the following morning with valises and with certain tools and accessories suited to architectural search and underground exploration.

column1: The morning of April 6th dawned clear
column2: and both explorers were at the bungalow by ten o'clock. Mr. Ward had the key
column3: and an entry and cursory survey were made. From the disordered condition of Dr. Allen's room it was obvious that the detectives had been there before
column4: and the later searchers hoped that they had found some clue which might prove of value. Of course the main business lay in the cellar; so thither they descended without much delay
column5: again making the circuit which each had vainly made before in the presence of the mad young owner. For a time everything seemed baffling
column6: each inch of the earthen floor and stone walls having so solid and innocuous an aspect that the thought of a yawning aperture was scarcely to be entertained. Willett reflected that since the original cellar was dug without knowledge of any catacombs beneath
column7: the beginning of the passage would represent the strictly modern delving of young Ward and his associates
column8: where they had probed for the ancient vaults whose rumour could have reached them by no wholesome means.

column1: The doctor tried to put himself in Charles's place to see how a delver would be likely to start
column2: but could not gain much inspiration from this method. Then he decided on elimination as a policy
column3: and went carefully over the whole subterranean surface both vertical and horizontal
column4: trying to account for every inch separately. He was soon substantially narrowed down
column5: and at last had nothing left but the small platform before the washtubs
column6: which he had tried once before in vain. Now experimenting in every possible way
column7: and exerting a double strength
column8: he finally found that the top did indeed turn and slide horizontally on a corner pivot. Beneath it lay a trim concrete surface with an iron manhole
column9: to which Mr. Ward at once rushed with excited zeal. The cover was not hard to lift
column10: and the father had quite removed it when Willett noticed the queerness of his aspect. He was swaying and nodding dizzily
column11: and in the gust of noxious air which swept up from the black pit beneath the doctor soon recognised ample cause.

column1: In a moment Dr. Willett had his fainting companion on the floor above and was reviving him with cold water. Mr. Ward responded feebly
column2: but it could be seen that the mephitic blast from the crypt had in some way gravely sickened him. Wishing to take no chances
column3: Willett hastened out to Broad Street for a taxicab and had soon dispatched the sufferer home despite his weak-voiced protests; after which he produced an electric torch
column4: covered his nostrils with a band of sterile gauze
column5: and descended once more to peer into the new-found depths. The foul air had now slightly abated
column6: and Willett was able to send a beam of light down the Stygian hole. For about ten feet
column7: he saw
column8: it was a sheer cylindrical drop with concrete walls and an iron ladder; after which the hole appeared to strike a flight of old stone steps which must originally have emerged to earth somewhat southwest of the present building.

column1: Willett freely admits that for a moment the memory of the old Curwen legends kept him from climbing down alone into that malodorous gulf. He could not help thinking of what Luke Fenner had reported on that last monstrous night. Then duty asserted itself and he made the plunge
column2: carrying a great valise for the removal of whatever papers might prove of supreme importance. Slowly
column3: as befitted one of his years
column4: he descended the ladder and reached the slimy steps below. This was ancient masonry
column5: his torch told him; and upon the dripping walls he saw the unwholesome moss of centuries. Down
column6: down
column7: ran the steps; not spirally
column8: but in three abrupt turns; and with such narrowness that two men could have passed only with difficulty. He had counted about thirty when a sound reached him very faintly; and after that he did not feel disposed to count any more.

column1: It was a godless sound; one of those low-keyed
column2: insidious outrages of Nature which are not meant to be. To call it a dull wail
column3: a doom-dragged whine
column4: or a hopeless howl of chorused anguish and stricken flesh without mind would be to miss its most quintessential loathsomeness and soul-sickening overtones. Was it for this that Ward had seemed to listen on that day he was removed? It was the most shocking thing that Willett had ever heard
column5: and it continued from no determinate point as the doctor reached the bottom of the steps and cast his torchlight around on lofty corridor walls surmounted by Cyclopean vaulting and pierced by numberless black archways. The hall in which he stood was perhaps fourteen feet high to the middle of the vaulting and ten or twelve feet broad. Its pavement was of large chipped flagstones
column6: and its walls and roof were of dressed masonry. Its length he could not imagine
column7: for it stretched ahead indefinitely into the blackness. Of the archways
column8: some had doors of the old six-panelled colonial type
column9: whilst others had none.

column1: Overcoming the dread induced by the smell and the howling
column2: Willett began to explore these archways one by one; finding beyond them rooms with groined stone ceilings
column3: each of medium size and apparently of bizarre uses. Most of them had fireplaces
column4: the upper courses of whose chimneys would have formed an interesting study in engineering. Never before or since had he seen such instruments or suggestions of instruments as here loomed up on every hand through the burying dust and cobwebs of a century and a half
column5: in many cases evidently shattered as if by the ancient raiders. For many of the chambers seemed wholly untrodden by modern feet
column6: and must have represented the earliest and most obsolete phases of Joseph Curwen's experimentation. Finally there came a room of obvious modernity
column7: or at least of recent occupancy. There were oil heaters
column8: bookshelves and tables
column9: chairs and cabinets
column10: and a desk piled high with papers of varying antiquity and contemporaneousness. Candlesticks and oil lamps stood about in several places; and finding a match-safe handy
column11: Willett lighted such as were ready for use.

column1: In the fuller gleam it appeared that this apartment was nothing less than the latest study or library of Charles Ward. Of the books the doctor had seen many before
column2: and a good part of the furniture had plainly come from the Prospect Street mansion. Here and there was a piece well known to Willett
column3: and the sense of familiarity became so great that he half forgot the noisomeness and the wailing
column4: both of which were plainer here than they had been at the foot of the steps. His first duty
column5: as planned long ahead
column6: was to find and seize any papers which might seem of vital importance; especially those portentous documents found by Charles so long ago behind the picture in Olney Court. As he searched he perceived how stupendous a task the final unravelling would be; for file on file was stuffed with papers in curious hands and bearing curious designs
column7: so that months or even years might be needed for a thorough deciphering and editing. Once he found large packets of letters with Prague and Rakus postmarks
column8: and in writing clearly recognisable as Orne's and Hutchinson's; all of which he took with him as part of the bundle to be removed in his valise.

column1: At last
column2: in a locked mahogany cabinet once gracing the Ward home
column3: Willett found the batch of old Curwen papers; recognising them from the reluctant glimpse Charles had granted him so many years ago. The youth had evidently kept them together very much as they had been when first he found them
column4: since all the titles recalled by the workmen were present except the papers addressed to Orne and Hutchinson
column5: and the cipher with its key. Willett placed the entire lot in his valise and continued his examination of the files. Since young Ward's immediate condition was the greatest matter at stake
column6: the closest searching was done among the most obviously recent matter; and in this abundance of contemporary manuscript one very baffling oddity was noted. The oddity was the slight amount in Charles's normal writing
column7: which indeed included nothing more recent than two months before. On the other hand
column8: there were literally reams of symbols and formulae
column9: historical notes and philosophical comment
column10: in a crabbed penmanship absolutely identical with the ancient script of Joseph Curwen
column11: though of undeniably modern dating. Plainly
column12: a part of the latter-day programme had been a sedulous imitation of the old wizard's writing
column13: which Charles seemed to have carried to a marvellous state of perfection. Of any third hand which might have been Allen's there was not a trace. If he had indeed come to be the leader
column14: he must have forced young Ward to act as his amanuensis.

column1: In this new material one mystic formula
column2: or rather pair of formulae
column3: recurred so often that Willett had it by heart before he had half finished his quest. It consisted of two parallel columns
column4: the left-hand one surmounted by the archaic symbol called ""Dragon's Head"" and used in almanacks to indicate the ascending node
column5: and the right-hand one headed by a corresponding sign of ""Dragon's Tail"" or descending node. The appearance of the whole was something like this
column6: and almost unconsciously the doctor realised that the second half was no more than the first written syllabically backward with the exception of the final monosyllables and of the odd name Yog-Sothoth
column7: which he had come to recognise under various spellings from other things he had seen in connexion with this horrible matter. The formulae were as follows - exactly so
column8: as Willett is abundantly able to testify - and the first one struck an odd note of uncomfortable latent memory in his brain
column9: which he recognised later when reviewing the events of that horrible Good Friday of the previous year.

column1: Y'AI 'NG'NGAH
YOG-SOTHOTH
H'EE - L'GEB
F'AI THRODOG
UAAAH
OGTHROD AI'F
GEB'L - EE'H
YOG-SOTHOTH
'NGAH'NG AI'Y
ZHRO
So haunting were these formulae
column2: and so frequently did he come upon them
column3: that before the doctor knew it he was repeating them under his breath. Eventually
column4: however
column5: he felt he had secured all the papers he could digest to advantage for the present; hence resolved to examine no more till he could bring the sceptical alienists en masse for an ampler and more systematic raid. He had still to find the hidden laboratory
column6: so leaving his valise in the lighted room he emerged again into the black noisome corridor whose vaulting echoed ceaselessly with that dull and hideous whine.

column1: The next few rooms he tried were all abandoned
column2: or filled only with crumbling boxes and ominous-looking leaden coffins; but impressed him deeply with the magnitude of Joseph Curwen's original operations. He thought of the slaves and seamen who had disappeared
column3: of the graves which had been violated in every part of the world
column4: and of what that final raiding party must have seen; and then he decided it was better not to think any more. Once a great stone staircase mounted at his right
column5: and he deduced that this must have reached to one of the Curwen outbuildings - perhaps the famous stone edifice with the high slit-like windows - provided the steps he had descended had led from the steep-roofed farmhouse. Suddenly the walls seemed to fall away ahead
column6: and the stench and the wailing grew stronger. Willett saw that he had come upon a vast open space
column7: so great that his torchlight would not carry across it; and as he advanced he encountered occasional stout pillars supporting the arches of the roof.

column1: After a time he reached a circle of pillars grouped like the monoliths of Stonehenge
column2: with a large carved altar on a base of three steps in the centre; and so curious were the carvings on that altar that he approached to study them with his electric light. But when he saw what they were he shrank away shuddering
column3: and did not stop to investigate the dark stains which discoloured the upper surface and had spread down the sides in occasional thin lines. Instead
column4: he found the distant wall and traced it as it swept round in a gigantic circle perforated by occasional black doorways and indented by a myriad of shallow cells with iron gratings and wrist and ankle bonds on chains fastened to the stone of the concave rear masonry. These cells were empty
column5: but still the horrible odour and the dismal moaning continued
column6: more insistent now than ever
column7: and seemingly varied at times by a sort of slippery thumping.

column1: From that frightful smell and that uncanny noise Willett's attention could no longer be diverted. Both were plainer and more hideous in the great pillared hall than anywhere else
column2: and carried a vague impression of being far below
column3: even in this dark nether world of subterrene mystery. Before trying any of the black archways for steps leading further down
column4: the doctor cast his beam of light about the stone-flagged floor. It was very loosely paved
column5: and at irregular intervals there would occur a slab curiously pierced by small holes in no definite arrangement
column6: while at one point there lay a very long ladder carelessly flung down. To this ladder
column7: singularly enough
column8: appeared to cling a particularly large amount of the frightful odour which encompassed everything. As he walked slowly about it suddenly occurred to Willett that both the noise and the odour seemed strongest directly above the oddly pierced slabs
column9: as if they might be crude trap-doors leading down to some still deeper region of horror. Kneeling by one
column10: he worked at it with his hands
column11: and found that with extreme difficulty he could budge it. At his touch the moaning beneath ascended to a louder key
column12: and only with vast trepidation did he persevere in the lifting of the heavy stone. A stench unnamable now rose up from below
column13: and the doctor's head reeled dizzily as he laid back the slab and turned his torch upon the exposed square yard of gaping blackness.

column1: If he had expected a flight of steps to some wide gulf of ultimate abomination
column2: Willett was destined to be disappointed; for amidst that foetor and cracked whining he discerned only the brick-faced top of a cylindrical well perhaps a yard and a half in diameter and devoid of any ladder or other means of descent. As the light shone down
column3: the wailing changed suddenly to a series of horrible yelps; in conjunction with which there came again that sound of blind
column4: futile scrambling and slippery thumping. The explorer trembled
column5: unwilling even to imagine what noxious thing might be lurking in that abyss
column6: but in a moment mustered up the courage to peer over the rough-hewn brink; lying at full length and holding the torch downward at arm's length to see what might lie below. For a second he could distinguish nothing but the slimy
column7: moss-grown brick walls sinking illimitably into that half-tangible miasma of murk and foulness and anguished frenzy; and then he saw that something dark was leaping clumsily and frantically up and down at the bottom of the narrow shaft
column8: which must have been from twenty to twenty-five feet below the stone floor where he lay. The torch shook in his hand
column9: but he looked again to see what manner of living creature might be immured there in the darkness of that unnatural well; left starving by young Ward through all the long month since the doctors had taken him away
column10: and clearly only one of a vast number prisoned in the kindred wells whose pierced stone covers so thickly studded in the floor of the great vaulted cavern. Whatever the things were
column11: they could not lie down in their cramped spaces; but must have crouched and whined and waited and feebly leaped all those hideous weeks since their master had abandoned them unheeded.

column1: But Marinus Bicknell Willett was sorry that he looked again; for surgeon and veteran of the dissecting-room though he was
column2: he has not been the same since. It is hard to explain just how a single sight of a tangible object with measureable dimensions could so shake and change a man; and we may only say that there is about certain outlines and entities a power of symbolism and suggestion which acts frightfully on a sensitive thinker's perspective and whispers terrible hints of obscure cosmic relationships and unnamable realities behind the protective illusions of common vision. In that second look Willett saw such an outline or entity
column3: for during the next few instants he was undoubtedly as stark mad as any inmate of Dr. Waite's private hospital. He dropped the electric torch from a hand drained of muscular power or nervous cordination
column4: nor heeded the sound of crunching teeth which told of its fate at the bottom of the pit. He screamed and screamed and screamed in a voice whose falsetto panic no acquaintance of his would ever have recognised; and though he could not rise to his feet he crawled and rolled desperately away over the damp pavement where dozens of Tartarean wells poured forth their exhausted whining and yelping to answer his own insane cries. He tore his hands on the rough
column5: loose stones
column6: and many times bruised his head against the frequent pillars
column7: but still he kept on. Then at last he slowly came to himself in the utter blackness and stench
column8: and stopped his ears against the droning wail into which the burst of yelping had subsided. He was drenched with perspiration and without means of producing a light; stricken and unnerved in the abysmal blackness and horror
column9: and crushed with a memory he never could efface. Beneath him dozens of those things still lived
column10: and from one of the shafts the cover was removed. He knew that what he had seen could never climb up the slippery walls
column11: yet shuddered at the thought that some obscure foot-hold might exist.

column1: What the thing was
column2: he would never tell. It was like some of the carvings on the hellish altar
column3: but it was alive. Nature had never made it in this form
column4: for it was too palpably unfinished. The deficiencies were of the most surprising sort
column5: and the abnormalities of proportion could not be described. Willett consents only to say that this type of thing must have represented entities which Ward called up from imperfect salts
column6: and which he kept for servile or ritualistic purposes. If it had not had a certain significance
column7: its image would not have been carved on that damnable stone. It was not the worst thing depicted on that stone - but Willett never opened the other pits. At the time
column8: the first connected idea in his mind was an idle paragraph from some of the old Curwen data he had digested long before; a phrase used by Simon or Jedediah Orne in that portentous confiscated letter to the bygone sorcerer: ""Certainely
column9: there was Noth'g butt ye liveliest Awfulness in that which H. rais'd upp from What he cou'd gather onlie a part of.""

column1: Then
column2: horribly supplementing rather than displacing this image
column3: there came a recollection of those ancient lingering rumours anent the burned
column4: twisted thing found in the fields a week after the Curwen raid. Charles Ward had once told the doctor what old Slocum said of that object; that it was neither thoroughly human
column5: nor wholly allied to any animal which Pawtuxet folk had ever seen or read about.

column1: These words hummed in the doctor's mind as he rocked to and fro
column2: squatting on the nitrous stone floor. He tried to drive them out
column3: and repeated the Lord's Prayer to himself; eventually trailing off into a mnemonic hodge-podge like the modernistic Waste Land of Mr. T. S. Eliot and finally reverting to the oft-repeated dual formula he had lately found in Ward's underground library: ""Y'ai 'ng'ngah
column4: Yog-Sothoth""
column5: and so on till the final underlined ""Zhro"". It seemed to soothe him
column6: and he staggered to his feet after a time; lamenting bitterly his fright-lost torch and looking wildly about for any gleam of light in the clutching inkiness of the chilly air. Think he would not; but he strained his eyes in every direction for some faint glint or reflection of the bright illumination he had left in the library. After a while he thought he detected a suspicion of a glow infinitely far away
column7: and toward this he crawled in agonised caution on hands and knees amidst the stench and howling
column8: always feeling ahead lest he collide with the numerous great pillars or stumble into the abominable pit he had uncovered.

column1: Once his shaking fingers touched something which he knew must be the steps leading to the hellish altar
column2: and from this spot he recoiled in loathing. At another time he encountered the pierced slab he had removed
column3: and here his caution became almost pitiful. But he did not come upon the dread aperture after all
column4: nor did anything issue from that aperture to detain him. What had been down there made no sound nor stir. Evidently its crunching of the fallen electric torch had not been good for it. Each time Willett's fingers felt a perforated slab he trembled. His passage over it would sometimes increase the groaning below
column5: but generally it would produce no effect at all
column6: since he moved very noiselessly. Several times during his progress the glow ahead diminished perceptibly
column7: and he realised that the various candles and lamps he had left must be expiring one by one. The thought of being lost in utter darkness without matches amidst this underground world of nightmare labyrinths impelled him to rise to his feet and run
column8: which he could safely do now that he had passed the open pit; for he knew that once the light failed
column9: his only hope of rescue and survival would lie in whatever relief party Mr. Ward might send after missing him for a sufficient period. Presently
column10: however
column11: he emerged from the open space into the narrower corridor and definitely located the glow as coming from a door on his right. In a moment he had reached it and was standing once more in young Ward's secret library
column12: trembling with relief
column13: and watching the sputterings of that last lamp which had brought him to safety.

column1: In another moment he was hastily filling the burned-out lamps from an oil supply he had previously noticed
column2: and when the room was bright again he looked about to see if he might find a lantern for further exploration. For racked though he was with horror
column3: his sense of grim purpose was still uppermost; and he was firmly determined to leave no stone unturned in his search for the hideous facts behind Charles Ward's bizarre madness. Failing to find a lantern
column4: he chose the smallest of the lamps to carry; also filling his pockets with candles and matches
column5: and taking with him a gallon can of oil
column6: which he proposed to keep for reserve use in whatever hidden laboratory he might uncover beyond the terrible open space with its unclean altar and nameless covered wells. To traverse that space again would require his utmost fortitude
column7: but he knew it must be done. Fortunately neither the frightful altar nor the opened shaft was near the vast cell-indented wall which bounded the cavern area
column8: and whose black mysterious archways would form the next goals of a logical search.

column1: So Willett went back to that great pillared hall of stench and anguished howling; turning down his lamp to avoid any distant glimpse of the hellish altar
column2: or of the uncovered pit with the pierced stone slab beside it. Most of the black doorways led merely to small chambers
column3: some vacant and some evidently used as storerooms; and in several of the latter he saw some very curious accumulations of various objects. One was packed with rotting and dust-draped bales of spare clothing
column4: and the explorer thrilled when he saw that it was unmistakably the clothing of a century and a half before. In another room he found numerous odds and ends of modern clothing
column5: as if gradual provisions were being made to equip a large body of men. But what he disliked most of all were the huge copper vats which occasionally appeared; these
column6: and the sinister incrustations upon them. He liked them even less than the weirdly figured leaden bowls whose rims retained such obnoxious deposits and around which clung repellent odours perceptible above even the general noisomeness of the crypt. When he had completed about half the entire circuit of the wall he found another corridor like that from which he had come
column7: and out of which many doors opened. This he proceeded to investigate; and after entering three rooms of medium size and of no significant contents
column8: he came at last to a large oblong apartment whose business-like tanks and tables
column9: furnaces and modern instruments
column10: occasional books and endless shelves of jars and bottles proclaimed it indeed the long-sought laboratory of Charles Ward - and no doubt of old Joseph Curwen before him.

column1: After lighting the three lamps which he found filled and ready
column2: Dr. Willett examined the place and all its appurtenances with the keenest interest; noting from the relative quantities of various reagents on the shelves that young Ward's dominant concern must have been with some branch of organic chemistry. On the whole
column3: little could be learned from the scientific ensemble
column4: which included a gruesome-looking dissecting table; so that the room was really rather a disappointment. Among the books was a tattered old copy of Borellus in black-letter
column5: and it was weirdly interesting to note that Ward had underlined the same passage whose marking had so perturbed good Mr. Merritt at Curwen's farmhouse more than a century and a half before. That older copy
column6: of course
column7: must have perished along with the rest of Curwen's occult library in the final raid. Three archways opened off the laboratory
column8: and these the doctor proceeded to sample in turn. From his cursory survey he saw that two led merely to small storerooms; but these he canvassed with care
column9: remarking the piles of coffins in various stages of damage and shuddering violently at two or three of the few coffin-plates he could decipher. There was much clothing also stored in these rooms
column10: and several new and tightly nailed boxes which he did not stop to investigate. Most interesting of all
column11: perhaps
column12: were some odd bits which he judged to be fragments of old Joseph Curwen's laboratory appliances. These had suffered damage at the hands of the raiders
column13: but were still partly recognisable as the chemical paraphernalia of the Georgian period.

column1: The third archway led to a very sizeable chamber entirely lined with shelves and having in the centre a table bearing two lamps. These lamps Willett lighted
column2: and in their brilliant glow studied the endless shelving which surrounded him. Some of the upper levels were wholly vacant
column3: but most of the space was filled with small odd-looking leaden jars of two general types; one tall and without handles like a Grecian lekythos or oil-jug
column4: and the other with a single handle and proportioned like a Phaleron jug. All had metal stoppers
column5: and were covered with peculiar-looking symbols moulded in low relief. In a moment the doctor noticed that these jugs were classified with great rigidity; all the lekythoi being on one side of the room with a large wooden sign reading ""Custodes"" above them
column6: and all the Phalerons on the other
column7: correspondingly labelled with a sign reading ""Materia"". Each of the jars or jugs
column8: except some on the upper shelves that turned out to be vacant
column9: bore a cardboard tag with a number apparently referring to a catalogue; and Willett resolved to look for the latter presently. For the moment
column10: however
column11: he was more interested in the nature of the array as a whole; and experimentally opened several of the lekythoi and Phalerons at random with a view to a rough generalisation. column1: But of the greatest immediate interest was the Orne material. It took Ward only a short time to prove from identity of penmanship a thing he had already considered established from the text of the letter to Curwen; namely
column2: that Simon Orne and his supposed son were one and the same person. As Orne had said to his correspondent
column3: it was hardly safe to live too long in Salem
column4: hence he resorted to a thirty-year sojourn abroad
column5: and did not return to claim his lands except as a representative of a new generation. Orne had apparently been careful to destroy most of his correspondence
column6: but the citizens who took action in 1771 found and preserved a few letters and papers which excited their wonder. There were cryptic formulae and diagrams in his and other hands which Ward now either copied with care or had photographed
column7: and one extremely mysterious letter in a chirography that the searcher recognised from items in the Registry of Deeds as positively Joseph Curwen's.

column1: This Curwen letter

column7: and furnace-tending services. To find

column1: Young Ward came home in a state of pleasant excitement
column2: and spent the following Saturday in a long and exhaustive study of the house in Olney Court. The place
column3: now crumbling with age

column5: with plain peaked roof
column6: large central chimney
column7: and artistically carved doorway with rayed fanlight
column8: triangular pediment
column9: and trim Doric pilasters. It had suffered but little alteration externally

column1: The present negro inhabitants were known to him
column2: and he was very courteously shewn about the interior by old Asa and his stout wife Hannah. Here there was more change than the outside indicated
column3: and Ward saw with regret that fully half of the fine scroll-and-urn overmantels and shell-carved cupboard linings were gone

column5: hacked
column6: and gouged
column7: or covered up altogether with cheap wall-paper. In general
column8: the survey did not yield as much as Ward had somehow expected; but it was at least exciting to stand within the ancestral walls which had housed such a man of horror as Joseph Curwen. He saw with a thrill that a monogram had been very carefully effaced from the ancient brass knocker.

column1: From then until after the close of school Ward spent his time on the photostatic copy of the Hutchinson cipher and the accumulation of local Curwen data. The former still proved unyielding; but of the latter he obtained so much
column2: and so many clues to similar data elsewhere
column3: that he was ready by July to make a trip to New London and New York to consult old letters whose presence in those places was indicated. This trip was very fruitful
column4: for it brought him the Fenner letters with their terrible description of the Pawtuxet farmhouse raid
column5: and the Nightingale-Talbot letters in which he learned of the portrait painted on a panel of the Curwen library. This matter of the portrait interested him particularly
column6: since he would have given much to know just what Joseph Curwen looked like; and he decided to make a second search of the house in Olney Court to see if there might not be some trace of the ancient features beneath peeling coats of later paint or layers of mouldy wall-paper.

column1: Early in August that search took place
column2: and Ward went carefully over the walls of every room sizeable enough to have been by any possibility the library of the evil builder. He paid especial attention to the large panels of such overmantels as still remained; and was keenly excited after about an hour
column3: when on a broad area above the fireplace in a spacious ground-floor room he became certain that the surface brought out by the peeling of several coats of paint was sensibly darker than any ordinary interior paint or the wood beneath it was likely to have been. A few more careful tests with a thin knife
column4: and he knew that he had come upon an oil portrait of great extent. With truly scholarly restraint the youth did not risk the damage which an immediate attempt to uncover the hidden picture with the knife might have done
column5: but just retired from the scene of his discovery to enlist expert help. In three days he returned with an artist of long experience
column6: Mr. Walter C. Dwight
column7: whose studio is near the foot of College Hill; and that accomplished restorer of paintings set to work at once with proper methods and chemical substances. Old Asa and his wife were duly excited over their strange visitors
column8: and were properly reimbursed for this invasion of their domestic hearth.

column1: As day by day the work of restoration progressed
column2: Charles Ward looked on with growing interest at the lines and shades gradually unveiled after their long oblivion. Dwight had begun at the bottom; hence since the picture was a three-quarter-length one
column3: the face did not come out for some time. It was meanwhile seen that the subject was a spare
column4: well-shaped man with dark-blue coat
column5: embroidered waistcoat
column6: black satin small-clothes
column7: and white silk stockings
column8: seated in a carved chair against the background of a window with wharves and ships beyond. When the head came out it was observed to bear a neat Albemarle wig
column9: and to possess a thin
column10: calm
column11: undistinguished face which seemed somehow familiar to both Ward and the artist. Only at the very last
column12: though
column13: did the restorer and his client begin to gasp with astonishment at the details of that lean
column14: pallid visage
column15: and to recognise with a touch of awe the dramatic trick which heredity had played. For it took the final bath of oil and the final stroke of the delicate scraper to bring out fully the expression which centuries had hidden; and to confront the bewildered Charles Dexter Ward
column16: dweller in the past
column17: with his own living features in the countenance of his horrible great-great-great-grandfather.

column1: Ward brought his parents to see the marvel he had uncovered
column2: and his father at once determined to purchase the picture despite its execution on stationary panelling. The resemblance to the boy

column5: though she could recall relatives who had some of the facial characteristics shared by her son and by the bygone Curwen. She did not relish the discovery
column6: and told her husband that he had better burn the picture instead of bringing it home. There was
column7: she averred
column8: something unwholesome about it; not only intrinsically
column9: but in its very resemblance to Charles. Mr. Ward
column10: however
column11: was a practical man of power and affairs - a cotton manufacturer with extensive mills at Riverpoint in the Pawtuxet Valley - and not one to listen to feminine scruples. The picture impressed him mightily with its likeness to his son

column13: it is needless to say

column1: It now remained to take off the panelling and remove it to the Ward home

column6: which must have lain directly behind the head of the portrait. Curious as to what such a space might mean or contain

column12: and proclaimed the volume as the ""Journall and Notes of Jos: Curwen
column13: Gent.
column14: of Providence-Plantations
column15: Late of Salem.""

column7: as the Hutchinson cipher which had hitherto baffled him. A third

column1: We have now reached the point from which the more academic school of alienists date Charles Ward's madness. Upon his discovery the youth had looked immediately at a few of the inner pages of the book and manuscripts
column2: and had evidently seen something which impressed him tremendously. Indeed
column3: in shewing the titles to the workmen he appeared to guard the text itself with peculiar care
column4: and to labour under a perturbation for which even the antiquarian and genealogical significance of the find could hardly account. Upon returning home he broke the news with an almost embarrassed air
column5: as if he wished to convey an idea of its supreme importance without having to exhibit the evidence itself. He did not even shew the titles to his parents
column6: but simply told them that he had found some documents in Joseph Curwen's handwriting
column7: ""mostly in cipher""
column8: which would have to be studied very carefully before yielding up their true meaning. It is unlikely that he would have shewn what he did to the workmen
column9: had it not been for their unconcealed curiosity. As it was he doubtless wished to avoid any display of peculiar reticence which would increase their discussion of the matter.

column1: That night Charles Ward sat up in his room reading the new-found book and papers
column2: and when day came he did not desist. His meals
column3: on his urgent request when his mother called to see what was amiss
column4: were sent up to him; and in the afternoon he appeared only briefly when the men came to install the Curwen picture and mantelpiece in his study. The next night he slept in snatches in his clothes
column5: meanwhile wrestling feverishly with the unravelling of the cipher manuscript. In the morning his mother saw that he was at work on the photostatic copy of the Hutchinson cipher
column6: which he had frequently shewn her before; but in response to her query he said that the Curwen key could not be applied to it. That afternoon he abandoned his work and watched the men fascinatedly as they finished their installation of the picture with its woodwork above a cleverly realistic electric log
column7: setting the mock-fireplace and overmantel a little out from the north wall as if a chimney existed
column8: and boxing in the sides with panelling to match the room's. The front panel holding the picture was sawn and hinged to allow cupboard space behind it. After the workmen went he moved his work into the study and sat down before it with his eyes half on the cipher and half on the portrait which stared back at him like a year-adding and century-recalling mirror.

column1: His parents
column2: subsequently recalling his conduct at this period
column3: give interesting details anent the policy of concealment which he practiced. Before servants he seldom hid any paper which he might be studying
column4: since he rightly assumed that Curwen's intricate and archaic chirography would be too much for them. With his parents
column5: however
column6: he was more circumspect; and unless the manuscript in question were a cipher
column7: or a mere mass of cryptic symbols and unknown ideographs (as that entitled ""To Him Who Shal Come After etc."" seemed to be)
column8: he would cover it with some convenient paper until his caller had departed. At night he kept the papers under lock and key in an antique cabinet of his
column9: where he also placed them whenever he left the room. He soon resumed fairly regular hours and habits
column10: except that his long walks and other outside interests seemed to cease. The opening of school
column11: where he now began his senior year
column12: seemed a great bore to him; and he frequently asserted his determination never to bother with college. He had
column13: he said
column14: important special investigations to make
column15: which would provide him with more avenues toward knowledge and the humanities than any university which the world could boast.

column1: Naturally
column2: only one who had always been more or less studious
column3: eccentric
column4: and solitary could have pursued this course for many days without attracting notice. Ward
column5: however
column6: was constitutionally a scholar and a hermit; hence his parents were less surprised than regretful at the close confinement and secrecy he adopted. At the same time

column8: nor give any connected account of such data as he had deciphered. This reticence he explained away as due to a wish to wait until he might announce some connected revelation

column1: During October Ward began visiting the libraries again
column2: but no longer for the antiquarian matter of his former days. Witchcraft and magic
column3: occultism and daemonology
column4: were what he sought now; and when Providence sources proved unfruitful he would take the train for Boston and tap the wealth of the great library in Copley Square
column5: the Widener Library at Harvard
column6: or the Zion Research Library in Brookline
column7: where certain rare works on Biblical subjects are available. He bought extensively

column1: About the middle of January
column3: there entered Ward's bearing an element of triumph which he did not explain
column4: and he was no more found at work upon the Hutchinson cipher. Instead

column6: and for the latter haunting all the sources of vital statistics in Providence. Local dealers in drugs and scientific supplies

column8: gave astonishingly queer and meaningless catalogues of the substances and instruments he purchased; but clerks at the State House

column10: and the various libraries agree as to the definite object of his second interest. He was searching intensely and feverishly for the grave of Joseph Curwen
column11: from whose slate slab an older generation had so wisely blotted the name.

column1: Little by little there grew upon the Ward family the conviction that something was wrong. Charles had had freaks and changes of minor interests before
column2: but this growing secrecy and absorption in strange pursuits was unlike even him. His school work was the merest pretence; and although he failed in no test
column3: it could be seen that the old application had all vanished. He had other concernments now; and when not in his new laboratory with a score of obsolete alchemical books
column4: could be found either poring over old burial records down town or glued to his volumes of occult lore in his study
column5: where the startlingly - one almost fancied increasingly - similar features of Joseph Curwen stared blandly at him from the great overmantel on the north wall.

column1: Late in March Ward added to his archive-searching a ghoulish series of rambles about the various ancient cemeteries of the city. The cause appeared later
column2: when it was learned from City Hall clerks that he had probably found an important clue. His quest had suddenly shifted from the grave of Joseph Curwen to that of one Naphthali Field; and this shift was explained when
column3: upon going over the files that he had been over
column4: the investigators actually found a fragmentary record of Curwen's burial which had escaped the general obliteration
column5: and which stated that the curious leaden coffin had been interred ""10 ft. S. and 5 ft. W. of Naphthali Field's grave in ye - "". The lack of a specified burying-ground in the surviving entry greatly complicated the search
column6: and Naphthali Field's grave seemed as elusive as that of Curwen; but here no systematic effacement had existed
column7: and one might reasonably be expected to stumble on the stone itself even if its record had perished. Hence the rambles - from which St. John's (the former King's) Churchyard and the ancient Congregational burying-ground in the midst of Swan Point Cemetery were excluded
column8: since other statistics had shewn that the only Naphthali Field (obiit 1729) whose grave could have been meant had been a Baptist.

column1: It was toward May when Dr. Willett
column2: at the request of the senior Ward
column3: and fortified with all the Curwen data which the family had gleaned from Charles in his non-secretive days
column4: talked with the young man. The interview was of little value or conclusiveness
column5: for Willett felt at every moment that Charles was thoroughly master of himself and in touch with matters of real importance; but it at least forced the secretive youth to offer some rational explanation of his recent demeanour. Of a pallid
column6: impassive type not easily shewing embarrassment
column7: Ward seemed quite ready to discuss his pursuits
column8: though not to reveal their object. He stated that the papers of his ancestor had contained some remarkable secrets of early scientific knowledge
column9: for the most part in cipher
column10: of an apparent scope comparable only to the discoveries of Friar Bacon and perhaps surpassing even those. They were
column11: however
column12: meaningless except when correlated with a body of learning now wholly obsolete; so that their immediate presentation to a world equipped only with modern science would rob them of all impressiveness and dramatic significance. To take their vivid place in the history of human thought they must first be correlated by one familiar with the background out of which they evolved
column13: and to this task of correlation Ward was now devoting himself. He was seeking to acquire as fast as possible those neglected arts of old which a true interpreter of the Curwen data must possess
column14: and hoped in time to make a full announcement and presentation of the utmost interest to mankind and to the world of thought. Not even Einstein
column15: he declared
column16: could more profoundly revolutionise the current conception of things.

column3: but the details of whose progress he did not relate

column5: he believed

column2: she is worried that allowing this kind of words will lead to bad language used by everybody in the future.

column1: Most scholars acknowledge that there are significant differences between AAVE and standard English.

column2: however

column1: The proponents of this view claim that the features of AAVE come from British or other white dialects.
They have come to be considered ""Black English"" because many black people moved from the south of the United States to the north.
What once were geographical differences in speech have now become ethnic differences.
Racial segregation may have helped this process by minimizing contact between whites and blacks.

Advocates of the other view of the origins of AAVE claim that many of its features are derived from an English Creole spoken by the first African Americans that came to the United States from West Africa.
Over the years
column2: this language has become more and more similar to standard English.

column1: Many features of AAVE can be found in Caribbean Creoles
column2: for example pronouncing this as dis.

column2: many features of AAVE are found in British dialects
column3: as well
column4: so it seems that both views of its origins are correct.

column1: Furthermore
column2: the English Creoles themselves are derived partly from British dialects
column3: as Trudgill points out (1983:61-70).

column1: The Oakland School Board Decision  In the last few years
column2: the educational implications of AAVE has been a topic of heated discussion in the United States.

column1: Many children who have grown up speaking AAVE have difficulties in school
column2: where they have to learn standard English before they can learn how to read and write.

column1: The massive educational failure of many African Americans students was the reason for the controversial decision taken by the Oakland school board in December 1996.

column2: many media commentators misunderstood the nature of the problem and stressed the significance of teaching African Americans standard English.

column2: and then switched to standard Swedish.

column1: A second set of students was taught entirely in standard Swedish for the same period.

\﻿ Granting Homosexual Couples the Right to Adopt  Recently an editorial that appeared in Svenska Dagbladet (1999-10-03) stated that homosexual couples must not be given the right to adopt children.
According to the writer
column2: adopted children are very vulnerable.

column1: They have been separated from their biological parents; they have often had several caretakers; and they have left their native country at an early age.
Growing up in a family that differs from other families would be adding to their trauma.
